# Keel
Status: complete
One-liner: A specification agent that turns a vague project prompt into a rigorous one by interrogating the ambiguities instead of guessing at them.

Stack: Streamlit, Python, Ollama Cloud, LLM orchestration
Live URL: https://qpjzctwb6nntdeaedg6zzr.streamlit.app
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/Keel

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
Most prompt-improvement tools do a one-shot rewrite: you hand them something vague and they hand back something longer, having silently invented every detail you left out. Keel refuses to do that. It reads a prompt, identifies what is genuinely underspecified — most often the input format and the expected output — and asks about those specifically, offering recommendations where a sensible default exists, then loops on confirmation before producing the final markdown spec. The harder decision was scope. The first version also generated project ideas and justified recommended tech stacks; both were cut. Three mediocre features read worse than one that works, and the clarification loop was the only part that solved a problem the user couldn't solve faster themselves. An earlier Python CLI build was abandoned entirely in favor of the Streamlit rewrite — a CLI meant nobody would ever try it. Because it's publicly deployed with a server-side key, it ships with per-session and daily caps plus an optional bring-your-own-key field.


## Metrics
- Scope: One feature, deliberately

## Anticipated questions
Q: Why ask questions instead of just writing a better prompt?
A: Because the missing information isn't recoverable. If a prompt doesn't say what the input looks like, no amount of rewriting produces that — it just produces a confident guess the user then has to detect and undo. Asking is cheaper than silently being wrong.

Q: Why did you cut two of the three features?
A: The idea-generation mode and the tech-stack justifier were both things a user could get elsewhere in thirty seconds. The clarification loop wasn't. Cutting them meant the one remaining feature got the attention it needed to actually be good.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)
- Stars: 0
- Last commit: 2026-09-03T14:04:05Z
- GitHub description: A prompt compiler for coding agents. Interrogates a vague idea through answerable questions, flags contradictions and infeasible combinations before you build, and is honest in the output about which decisions were yours vs. its own

## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub)
- Python: 379223
- CSS: 2781

## README
# ⛵ Keel

Keel takes a vague, one-line software project idea, asks a short series of targeted
clarifying questions about what the idea leaves unstated, and produces a structured,
downloadable markdown prompt you can paste into a coding agent (Claude Code, Cursor,
Copilot).

It is a single-page [Streamlit](https://streamlit.io) app.

## Run it locally

```
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .streamlit/secrets.toml.example .streamlit/secrets.toml   # then add one key
streamlit run app.py
```

`.streamlit/secrets.toml` holds your API key server-side and is gitignored. Keel supports
three providers and picks the first key it finds, in this order:

1. `GROQ_API_KEY` — Groq Cloud (`openai/gpt-oss-120b`)
2. `OLLAMA_API_KEY` — Ollama Cloud (`gpt-oss:120b`)
3. `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` — Anthropic (`claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`)

Set `KEEL_MODEL` to override the model for whichever provider is active. The app still
runs with no key — degraded, clearly labelled, using template defaults. The sidebar also
takes a per-session key for any of the three providers.

`FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` is optional — it powers the "reference for structure" feature
([Firecrawl](https://firecrawl.dev)). Without it, that input is disabled and everything
else works unchanged.

### Local Ollama for development

Prompt iteration (especially the synthesis prompt) burns hosted quota fast. For local
work, point Keel at an Ollama daemon:

```
ollama serve                                  # in another terminal
ollama pull qwen3:14b                          # or any capable instruct model
KEEL_PROVIDER=ollama streamlit run app.py
```

`KEEL_PROVIDER` is read from the OS environment **or** from a line in
`.streamlit/secrets.toml` (`KEEL_PROVIDER = "ollama"`) — pin it there and every `streamlit
run` / `python evals/run_evals.py` uses the local daemon with no per-command export.

`KEEL_PROVIDER=ollama` uses `http://localhost:11434` with no API key. Override the model
with `KEEL_OLLAMA_MODEL` (default `qwen3:14b`; the app also accepts `KEEL_MODEL`). Keel
sends `think=False` on local calls so a reasoning model does not spend its whole token
budget on hidden chain-of-thought and return empty JSON — harmless for plain instruct
models. If nothing answers on localhost the error says so — it never silently pretends the
call worked, and the deployed app never takes this path unless a deployer sets that env
var.

**Caveat:** a small local model produces noticeably weaker synthesis than the hosted
models. Use Ollama to iterate on plumbing, flow, and prompt *structure* — but validate
final output quality against a hosted model before judging a prompt change good. Do not
tune the synthesis prompt exclusively against local output.

`KEEL_PROVIDER` also accepts `groq`, `ollama-cloud`, or `anthropic` to force a specific
hosted provider instead of the key-presence default.

### Smoke-test the model connection

```
python doctor.py                        # provider auto-picked from env / secrets.toml
python doctor.py --provider groq        # force a hosted provider
KEEL_PROVIDER=ollama python doctor.py   # test the local daemon
```

Makes exactly one live LLM call and prints the raw failure reason if it fails. Run this
before deploying — it is the check the previous build lacked.

## The slot model

A **slot** is a named dimension a prompt must pin down. Keel asks a question because a
slot is empty and stops when every required slot is addressed — termination is a loop
over the slot list, never "the model decides it has asked enough."

| Slot | Captures | Tier |
|---|---|---|
| `io_contract` | What goes in, what comes out, in what format | core |
| `scale` | Volume, frequency, data size | core |
| `runtime` | Where it runs — CLI, cron, server, notebook, browser | core |
| `constraints` | Hard limits: offline, no paid APIs, language, existing deps | core |
| `done` | Observable definition of done | core |
| `non_goals` | What the agent must NOT build | core |
| `data_model` | The core entities and the fields each record carries | optional |
| `interfaces` | The concrete surface: endpoints, commands, screens, functions | optional |
| `error_handling` | What happens on bad input, failure, or partial success | optional |
| `auth_model` | Sign-in policy (no login / password+sessions / password+tokens / external) — policy only, never security parameters | optional |
| `seed_data` | Whether the project ships with data (empty / examples / full sample / from a file) | optional |

`auth_model` and `seed_data` are low-priority: never asked as questions, always
`keel_decided` from their `choices` (or `template_default` with no LLM). `auth_model`
carries a `skip_if` that suppresses it entirely — not asked, not defaulted, not
rendered — when the `non_goals` answer already rules authentication out.

An **audience mode** toggle on the start screen decides how questions are asked:

- **Guided** (default) assumes no software background. It asks only the six core
  slots, ignores the depth selector, phrases `runtime` / `scale` / `constraints`
  as plain-language multiple choice (plus "Something else" and "I'm not sure"),
  and shows a *Why does this matter?* note under every question. Everything not
  asked is defaulted — closed-answer slots become `keel_decided`, open ones
  `llm_default`.
- **Technical** keeps today's terse free-text questions and the **Depth**
  selector: `Quick` asks the six core, `Standard` (default) adds `data_model` and
  `interfaces`, `Thorough` adds `error_handling`.

Every question also offers **Decide for me** (records the value as `keel_decided`
with a reason) alongside **Skip this** (leaves it open). No session asks more than
**8** questions; any slot not asked is filled from the answers already given (one
LLM call), never left blank.

Slots live in YAML under [`keel/templates/`](keel/templates/) — `default`, `cli`,
`data-pipeline`, `web-api`, `web-app`. Templates differ in question phrasing, priority,
and section mapping (`web-app` is for browser-facing apps and never lists a UI as a
non-goal; `web-api` is reserved for HTTP services). Keel picks one by keyword heuristic on
your idea, preferring `default` when the prompt is ambiguous; a dropdown lets you override.

Each slot carries a `default_text` (a concrete human-readable fallback answer), a
`default_strategy` (an instruction used *only* inside the LLM prompt to generate a
context-aware default; never rendered — there is a test that asserts it), a hand-written
`why_this_matters` note, and — for the closed-answer slots — a hand-written `choices`
list (`label`, `plain_language`, `tradeoff`). The choice and why text are static: no
LLM call, identical between runs.

## Architecture

```
app.py                    Streamlit UI and flow control only
keel/models.py            pydantic models
keel/engine.py            slot state machine, template loading, the capped LLM helper
keel/render.py            synthesis pass + deterministic fallback -> markdown
keel/llm.py               the one place an LLM is called; returns (result, error)
keel/session_io.py        session <-> JSON, schema-version gate + migrations (v1 -> v3)
keel/firecrawl.py         stdlib HTTP client for the Firecrawl scrape / map API
keel/reference.py         reference intake: scraped markdown -> evidence -> slot candidates
keel/mockup.py            optional static wireframe: LLM HTML -> allowlist sanitizer
keel/templates/*.yaml     five slot templates
.streamlit/config.toml    dark theme palette
assets/style.css          the CSS the theme block can't reach (chips, conflict banner)
doctor.py                 one-live-call smoke script
tests/
```

`keel/engine.py`, `keel/render.py`, `keel/session_io.py`, `keel/firecrawl.py`,
`keel/reference.py`, and `keel/mockup.py` import and pass their tests without Streamlit
installed.

The result screen renders the spec section by section (each collapsible), shows a conflict
banner above it when `check_conflicts` found anything, and colour-codes every answer by
where it came from — the same chips appear in the sidebar progress panel, which tracks each
slot's state live through the session.

### LLM integration

All calls go through `keel/llm.complete_json(system, user, *, provider, max_tokens)`,
which returns a `(result, error)` tuple — never a bare `None`, never a raised exception.
`provider` is a `Provider(name, api_key, model, host)`; `llm.resolve_provider(secrets)`
builds one. Groq and Ollama enforce JSON natively; Anthropic via an assistant-turn prefill
— a prose reply becomes a distinguishable parse error. On failure the UI surfaces the
reason and falls back to template text.

Every answer carries a **source**: `extracted` (from your idea), `asked` (you typed it),
`reference` (confirmed from a scraped reference — see below), `llm_default` (the model
suggested it and you accepted), `template_default` (static YAML fallback, the model was
unavailable), `keel_decided` (you pressed **Decide for me** — Keel chose and recorded a
one-line reason plus a *revisit this if …* condition, both surfaced in the
*Decisions Keel made for you* section), or `skipped` (you left it deliberately open).
`SessionState.degraded` is *derived* from that state — it is true only when a slot is on
`template_default`, or the synthesis or conflict-check call actually failed; `keel_decided`
is not a degradation. A transient earlier error that did not change the finished document
(a missed extraction, one re-tried question) does not trip the banner.

The sidebar never shows a bare `n / n resolved`: it breaks the count into
`answered · Keel decided · skipped · pending`, so a spec that is mostly Keel's choices
reads as exactly that.

Call sites, all routed through `engine.capped_complete_json` (per-session cap of 14):

1. **Extract** pre-answered slots from the opening idea.
2. **Question** — generate one question + recommended default per unfilled slot (at most 8).
3. **Context defaults** — one call that fills any slot the depth or the 8-question cap left
   unasked, from the answers already given.
4. **Conflict check** (`render.check_conflicts`) — its own call, *before* synthesis, looking
   for contradictions between answers and for a capability in the original idea that no
   answer covers (premise drift). Its result is written into *Open questions* mechanically
   in Python; the synthesis model never decides whether a conflict is reported.
5. **Synthesis** — once, after every slot is filled: one call that reads the idea plus
   every answer and writes the whole document. It keeps each section consistent with the
   most specific answer, moves facts to the right section, enumerates the full interface
   surface, and expands each section to the length its content warrants. Section headings
   and their order are owned by `render.py` (`SECTION_ORDER`), never the model: the model
   returns section *bodies* keyed by name. It also returns `resolved_conflicts` — which of
   the contradictions it was handed its document silenced, and how.

The document's sections, in order: Context, Objective, Input / Output contract,
Constraints, Acceptance criteria, **Build order** (3–6 dependency-ordered stages with a
verification line each), **Project structure** (a suggested file tree, labelled not a
requirement), **Decisions Keel made for you** (one entry per `keel_decided` slot — the
choice, the reason, a *revisit this if …* clause; omitted when empty), Non-goals, Open
questions. `Build order` and `Project structure` come from the synthesis call and are
suppressed at `Quick` depth; `Decisions Keel made for you` is assembled in Python. A
one-sentence footer notes the spec benefits from review by someone with software
experience.

After synthesis, each pre-synthesis conflict is **re-validated against the document that
was actually produced** (`render._revalidate_conflicts`). A conflict the model reported
resolving — or a premise-drift conflict the finished document now plainly covers — moves
to a *Resolved during synthesis* list (shown in the UI, never in *Open questions*). Only
conflicts that survive re-validation reach *Open questions*. Anything the model claims to
have resolved that was never raised, or resolved without reporting, is logged.

The conflict check reports two kinds. A **`logical`** conflict is a direct
contradiction between answers, or the idea, that the developer has to resolve. A
**`feasibility`** conflict is a combination that cannot work in practice even though no
single answer is wrong — a single-process development server behind "hundreds of
concurrent users", storage that cannot carry the stated concurrency — and usually means
one answer needs revising, not that the developer contradicted themselves; it renders
distinctly (`**Feasibility (…)**` with a *Likely fix*).

The synthesized document is then run through deterministic Python checks (no extra LLM
call): structure and ordering, empty sections, hardcoded-secret scrub (with a note added
to *Open questions*), a `default_strategy`-leak assertion, acceptance criteria that
merely restate a constraint or non-goal, and a missing disclaimer in a
health/legal/financial spec. **Every numeric literal in the rendered document must trace
to an answer** (verbatim or a plain arithmetic derivation of one); a capacity, throughput,
or volume figure that does not is rewritten qualitatively and listed under *Open
questions*. **Non-goals** are tightened — any bullet that hedges ("not a focus", "beyond
basic", "kept minimal") is dropped and the list is capped at eight. Any structural failure
falls back to the deterministic one-value-per-line renderer, with a visible warning and
the degraded note (`synthesis_failed` is set). That renderer stays fully functional with
no LLM available.

*Open questions* is rebuilt in Python as up to three labelled subsections, each omitted
when empty: **Unresolved conflicts** (survivors of re-validation, plus a
check-unavailable note), **Not specified** (slots the user deliberately skipped), and
**Worth deciding before starting** (synthesis-identified gaps, the numeric rewrites, the
restatement and sensitive-domain flags). `keel_decided` slots never appear here — they
own the *Decisions* section. When all three subsections are empty the section reads
"None — every dimension was addressed", and a test asserts that line never renders beside
a non-empty conflict list.

### Caps (all constants)

| Cap | Value | Where |
|---|---|---|
| LLM calls per session | 20 | `keel/engine.py` |
| Questions asked per session | 8 | `keel/engine.py` |
| Regenerations per session | 3 | `keel/engine.py` |
| Output tokens — question | 800 | `keel/llm.py` |
| Output tokens — synthesis | 4500 | `keel/render.py` |
| Output tokens — wireframe | 4000 | `keel/mockup.py` |
| Shared-key calls per day | 500 | `app.py` |
| Opening prompt length | 500 chars | `keel/engine.py` |

Past the daily ceiling the shared key is disabled and users are directed to supply their
own via the sidebar **API key** field (used for that session only, never stored).

## Reference for structure

When you have only a rough notion ("something like Trello"), a blank slot page is hard to
answer. In the reference field on the start screen, give Keel either a **URL** or a
**product name**:

- a **URL** is scraped directly;
- a **name** ("something like Harvest") is searched first ([Firecrawl](https://firecrawl.dev)
  `/v1/search`), and you pick which of the top results is the real site — a wrong
  resolution silently poisoning every slot is the main failure mode, so the choice is
  always yours.

Either way Keel then scrapes for *structure only* — via Firecrawl, keyed from
`FIRECRAWL_API_KEY` in secrets — entities, screens and endpoints, primary flows, and the
features a first build would deliberately skip. One LLM call turns that into candidate slot
values.

You can also **upload a screenshot or a hand-drawn sketch** of a UI (PNG/JPEG/WebP, ≤ 4 MB).
A vision model reads the screens, form fields, and navigation — structure only, no copy or
branding. This needs a multimodal model: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (Claude Haiku is multimodal),
a local Ollama vision model (`KEEL_PROVIDER=ollama`), or `KEEL_VISION_MODEL` naming a vision
model on your Groq key. Without one, the image field is disabled and says why — the default
Groq model (`openai/gpt-oss-120b`) is text-only.

Nothing enters the spec unconfirmed. A confirm step shows every candidate with the
reference phrases it came from; you keep, edit, or drop each one (clear the box to drop it).
Kept values fill their slot with source `reference`; the rest of the slots are asked as
normal. The source URL is recorded in *Open questions* so the provenance travels with the
document — product names, wording, and visual design are never carried across.

A reference costs one Firecrawl fetch (a thin landing page triggers up to two more
structural sub-pages, hard-capped at three) plus one LLM call, both counted against the
session caps. Non-HTTP schemes, IP literals, and loopback / internal hosts are refused
before anything is fetched. Every reference mode is optional; the blank-prompt flow is the
default and works with Firecrawl unavailable. `keel/firecrawl.py` (the HTTP client, stdlib
only) and `keel/reference.py` (evidence → candidates → slots) import and test without
Streamlit.

## Wireframe preview

The result screen has an opt-in **Generate wireframe preview** button. It makes one extra
LLM call that turns the `interfaces` and `data_model` answers into a greyscale, static HTML
sketch — one block per screen with its route and fields — so you can eyeball the structure.
It is not part of the spec and is offered as a separate `.html` download.

Keel does not execute generated code, ever. The model's HTML is untrusted: `keel/mockup.py`
rebuilds it from a tag/attribute **allowlist**, dropping `<script>`, `on*` handlers,
`<iframe>`/`<object>`/`<embed>`, `<form action>`, `<style>`, `<img>`, and any
`javascript:` / `data:` / external URL. The sanitized result is framed with
`st.components.v1.html` and wrapped in a fixed greyscale stylesheet. An injected `<script>`
in the model's response is stripped — there is a test that proves it.

## Save, edit, regenerate

The result screen offers **Download session (.json)** next to Download .md. The file holds
the whole session — prompt, template, depth, every answer with its `source`, the conflict
list, the call count, and a `schema_version` — and nothing else; Keel never stores a session
server-side. **Resume a saved session** on the start screen loads one back and drops you at
the review step (a file from a newer Keel is refused with a clear message rather than
half-read).

The review step lists every dimension that fed the spec, each editable, tagged with where
it came from (`from your idea` / `you answered` / `Keel suggested` / `template fallback` /
`skipped`). **Regenerate spec** re-runs the conflict check and synthesis from the edited
answers — no question is ever re-asked. Each regeneration costs two calls and is capped (`engine.MAX_REGENERATIONS`); the
UI shows how many are left. `keel/session_io.py` owns the format; it imports and tests
without Streamlit.

## Deploy to Streamlit Community Cloud

Point a new app at `app.py`, set one of `GROQ_API_KEY` / `OLLAMA_API_KEY` /
`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (and optionally `KEEL_MODEL`) in the app's **Secrets**, and deploy.
`requirements.txt` pins the dependencies. Do **not** set `KEEL_PROVIDER=ollama` on a
deployed app — there is no local daemon there and every call will fail loudly.

## Evals

```
python evals/run_evals.py                       # provider auto-picked; writes evals/RESULTS.md
KEEL_PROVIDER=ollama python evals/run_evals.py  # local model — no hosted quota, for iteration
python evals/run_evals.py --persona deterministic --limit 3   # fast partial pass
```

[`evals/cases.json`](evals/cases.json) holds ~15 hand-labelled vague prompts: for each, the
slots a competent engineer would insist on pinning down, a persona for the simulated user,
the facts the prompt already states, and any contradiction `check_conflicts` should catch.
[`evals/simulated_user.py`](evals/simulated_user.py) answers each question in character (or,
with no provider, accepts the recommendation and skips on a fixed schedule).

`run_evals.py` runs every case end to end and writes `evals/RESULTS.md`. Commit that file
when you tune a prompt, so the next run's diff shows what moved. Metrics are pure Python, no
judge model: slot coverage, mean questions asked, missed-ambiguity rate, redundancy rate,
conflict recall, and false-precision rate (numbers in the spec that trace to no answer). The
table stamps the model and persona mode that produced it.

[`evals/fixtures/`](evals/fixtures/) holds frozen sessions used as permanent regression
cases; `run_evals.py` exits non-zero if any of them regresses. Two are contradiction
cases — the hotel-website "no UI" case and the health-monitoring "offline but
AI-generated" case. One is a **feasibility** case (`feasibility-devserver-concurrency`):
a development server plus company-wide concurrency must produce a `feasibility` conflict.
One is a **numeric-honesty** case (`qualitative-only`): every answer is qualitative, so
the rendered spec must contain no invented capacity or throughput figure. Re-run them
after any edit to the question, conflict, or synthesis prompt. Rebuild the two
contradiction fixtures with `python evals/fixtures/build_fixtures.py` only if the slot
taxonomy changes.

The committed `RESULTS.md` records which model and persona mode produced it. A small local
model scores differently from a hosted one — iterate locally, but regenerate the committed
table against the hosted model before trusting the numbers.

## Tests

```
pip install pytest
pytest
```

# ML-Agent (ML Pipeline Architect)
Status: complete
One-liner: A multi-agent system that builds, trains, and self-heals an end-to-end ML pipeline from a single problem statement, running on local LLMs.

Stack: Ollama, multi-agent orchestration, Python, scikit-learn
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/ML-Agent

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
The interesting problem here isn't code generation, it's recovery. An agent that writes a training script and hands it over is trivial; an agent that runs the script, reads the traceback, diagnoses whether the failure was a schema assumption, a dtype issue, or a genuinely bad modeling choice, and then fixes the right layer, is not. The self-healing loop is the project. Running it on local models via Ollama rather than a frontier API was a constraint that improved the design. Local models drift and hallucinate more under long, loosely-structured prompts, which forced hard structure on the control flow — narrow agent responsibilities, explicit state, validated handoffs — rather than relying on a strong model to hold a vague plan together.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)
- Stars: 1
- Last commit: 2026-08-24T14:07:34Z
- GitHub description: AI agent that automatically builds, trains, and self-heals end-to-end ML pipelines from a single problem statement using local LLMs via Ollama.

## README
# 🤖 ML Pipeline Architect — Multi-Agent System

An end-to-end autonomous Machine Learning engineering agent framework powered by local LLMs via Ollama. This project orchestrates a team of **9 specialized agents** to analyze problems, hunt down datasets, clean schemas, plan preprocessing, select models, generate python pipelines, run validation code, auto-debug errors, and compile comprehensive evaluation reports—all from a sleek, real-time web dashboard or a CLI.

---

## 🚀 Key Features

*   **Multi-Agent Collaborative Architecture**: Uses **Ollama** locally to drive communication between specialized roles using optimal models (e.g., `gemma4:latest` for analytical orchestrations and `qwen2.5-coder:14b` for robust code gen).
*   **Intelligent Dataset Hunting**: Searches the web dynamically (DuckDuckGo, HuggingFace, UCI Repository) or fetches relevant datasets from Kaggle using credentials. Supports direct local CSV upload or URLs.
*   **Automatic Schema Profiling & Preprocessing**: Infers columns, checks target balance, and designs standard scaler/encoder/imputation strategies automatically.
*   **Self-Correction Code Debugger Loop**: If the generated machine learning training script crashes, the *DebuggerAgent* captures the traceback and rewrites the script iteratively (up to a custom maximum retry count).
*   **Interactive Web UI & Real-Time Log Streaming**: A premium dashboard built with Flask and Vanilla CSS/JS featuring smooth animations, live logs, progress timelines, and final model evaluation reports.
*   **CLI Mode**: Full-featured programmatic CLI terminal interface for head-less pipeline executions.

---

## 🗺️ System Workflow

The project utilizes a state-machine design directed by an **Orchestrator** agent to transition between pipeline stages:

```mermaid
graph TD
    User[User Problem Statement] --> Analyst[ProblemAnalystAgent]
    Analyst --> Hunter[DatasetHunterAgent]
    Hunter --> Inspector[SchemaInspectorAgent]
    Inspector --> Planner[PreprocessingPlannerAgent]
    Planner --> Selector[ModelSelectorAgent]
    Selector --> Generator[CodeGeneratorAgent]
    Generator --> Executor[ExecutorValidatorAgent]
    Executor -- Failure / Traceback --> Debugger[DebuggerAgent]
    Debugger -- Self-Correction / Rewrites --> Executor
    Executor -- Success / Metrics Generated --> Reporter[ReportAgent]
    Reporter --> Report[Final HTML/Markdown Report & Artifacts]
```

---

## 🛠️ Prerequisites & Setup

### 1. Install & Configure Ollama
Ensure you have [Ollama](https://ollama.com) installed and running locally.

Pull the required models used by the agents:
```bash
# General analysis, orchestration & reporting
ollama pull gemma4:latest

# Code generation & debugging
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:14b
```

### 2. Python Environment Setup
Clone or download this repository, navigate to the folder, and run:

```bash
# Create virtual environment
python -m venv venv

# Activate virtual environment (Windows)
venv\Scripts\activate

# Activate virtual environment (macOS/Linux)
source venv/bin/activate

# Install dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

### 3. Kaggle API Key Configuration (Optional)
To enable automated Kaggle dataset downloads during dataset hunting:
1. Go to your Kaggle Account Settings.
2. Click **Create New API Token** to download `kaggle.json`.
3. Place the `kaggle.json` file in the root folder of this project.

---

## 💻 How to Run

### Option A: The Web Dashboard (Recommended)
Launch the Flask development server:
```bash
python app.py
```
Open [http://localhost:5000](http://localhost:5000) in your web browser. You'll be greeted by an interactive UI to describe your ML task, upload a dataset, and follow the multi-agent execution timeline with live streamed logs.

### Option B: The CLI Interface
For a text-based terminal pipeline execution:
```bash
python main.py
```
Follow the interactive prompts to define your ML problem and view raw log dumps of each agent's execution.

---

## 📂 Project Structure

```text
├── agents/                      # Specialized agent prompt templates & class implementations
│   ├── base_agent.py            # Base agent wrapping Ollama requests and JSON parsing logic
│   ├── orchestrator.py          # State machine and controller driving the agent pipeline
│   ├── problem_analyst.py       # Determines problem domain and ML objective
│   ├── dataset_hunter.py        # Searches UCI, Kaggle, and Web for data
│   ├── schema_inspector.py      # Profiles columns, missing ratios, and class balance
│   ├── preprocessing_planner.py  # Outlines transformation, scaling, and encoding rules
│   ├── model_selector.py        # Selects appropriate target models (e.g., XGBoost, RandomForest)
│   ├── code_generator.py        # Generates clean training and prediction code
│   ├── executor_validator.py    # Runs pipeline scripts safely and monitors logs
│   ├── debugger.py              # Debugs execution failure tracebacks
│   └── report.py                # Generates final evaluation artifacts
├── models/                      # Typed schemas and data structures for serialization
├── static/                      # Styling and Javascript front-end logic for the dashboard
├── templates/                   # Jinja HTML UI templates
├── outputs/                     # Generated training/prediction scripts, metrics, and models
├── app.py                       # Flask entrypoint server
├── main.py                      # CLI entrypoint script
├── requirements.txt             # Project requirements list
└── README.md                    # This document
```

---

## 📊 Benchmark

`bench/` measures this agent end-to-end against real baselines on 15 datasets pinned from OpenML (`python -m bench.run`, then `python -m bench.report`): a majority/median floor, a hand-built LightGBM baseline (standard encoding, no tuning), AutoGluon (`medium_quality`), and FLAML — all on identical splits and seeds, each run isolated in its own subprocess with a timeout and memory cap. Every run appends to `bench/results.db` with a timestamp and git SHA, so nothing is overwritten and regressions are traceable across commits. `bench/RESULTS.md` reports win/tie/loss by non-overlapping bootstrap confidence intervals (never point estimates alone), per-dataset metrics, cost per point of improvement, and a full failure-mode taxonomy.

**Limitations, stated plainly**: 15 datasets is a small sample — read results as directional, not definitive. 12 of the 15 come from OpenML-CC18, which is clean, pre-curated tabular data, not representative of the messy, real-world datasets this agent will actually meet. AutoGluon's `medium_quality` preset trades accuracy for speed; `best_quality` would likely close some of the gap shown here. The agent's generated pipelines expose no reusable inference path, so held-out scoring required reproducing their (deterministic) preprocessing externally — see `bench/competitors/agent_competitor.py` for exactly what that means for the numbers.

---

## ⚠️ Notes & Best Practices

*   **Ollama Speed**: Execution speed depends heavily on your hardware capabilities (especially CPU/GPU memory). Ensure Ollama has enough resources allocated to avoid connection timeouts.
*   **Output Location**: Code, trained model weights, evaluation plots, and metadata are saved inside the dynamically created `outputs/` folder inside the workspace directory.

# DataSleuth
Status: complete
One-liner: A fully local multi-agent data analyst with a Critic that independently re-executes generated code to catch hallucinated results.

Stack: LangGraph, Ollama, qwen3:14b, qwen2.5-coder:14b, FastAPI, SSE, SQLite
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/DataSleuth

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
LLM data-analysis agents fail in a specific, dangerous way: the model writes analysis code, reports a plausible number, and the number is wrong — either because the code silently errored or because the model narrated a result it never actually computed. Self-critique prompting doesn't catch this, because the same model that hallucinated the result is being asked whether it hallucinated the result. So the Critic node doesn't review the reasoning, it re-executes the code independently and compares. Verification is grounded in execution rather than in a second opinion from the same weights. LangGraph with SQLite checkpointing handles the state machine and makes runs resumable; FastAPI with SSE streams intermediate steps so the user watches the analysis happen rather than staring at a spinner. Whole thing runs on an RTX 5070 with no external API calls, which matters for anyone who can't send their data to a vendor.


## Metrics
- External API calls: Zero — fully local

## Anticipated questions
Q: Why not just let the model check its own work?
A: Because self-critique shares the failure mode it's meant to catch. If the model believed a wrong number the first time, asking it to review the number gets you the same belief with more confidence attached. The Critic re-runs the code — execution is a ground truth the model can't talk its way around.

Q: Why local models instead of GPT-4-class ones?
A: Data analysis usually means the data is sensitive. A system that can't run on-premise doesn't get used for the cases that matter most.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)
- Stars: 0
- Last commit: 2026-08-10T13:51:03Z
- GitHub description: Multi-agent AI data analyst that profiles datasets, generates hypotheses, writes analysis code, and self-corrects — with a Critic agent that rejects hallucinated or statistically invalid conclusions. LangGraph + Ollama, fully local.

## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub)
- Python: 111786
- HTML: 14241
- JavaScript: 11708
- CSS: 9593

## README
# DataSleuth

A fully local multi-agent data analysis system. Upload a messy CSV/TSV/XLSX;
a team of agents ingests it, profiles it, proposes hypotheses, writes and
runs code to test them, **independently re-verifies every result before
it's allowed to count**, charts what survives, and writes a cited report —
including an honest list of what it checked and rejected.

Everything runs on local Ollama models. No cloud APIs, no data leaves the
machine.

## Why the Critic matters

Every other step in this pipeline can be fooled by an LLM that's
confidently wrong. The Critic is the gate that catches it:

1. **Re-execution, not self-report.** The Critic never trusts the Coder's
   claimed output — it re-runs the exact same code in a fresh subprocess
   and compares `code_hash` + the result JSON. A mismatch is an automatic
   reject, no LLM judgment call needed.
2. **Independent scrutiny.** Only after reproducibility is confirmed does a
   low-temperature reasoning pass check the *evidence* against the *claim*:
   wrong statistical test, p-value that doesn't clear significance, a
   conclusion drawn from a column that's mostly null, a leakage column
   masquerading as a real driver, correlation dressed up as causation.
3. **Nothing hides.** Rejected hypotheses aren't discarded — they're logged
   to the trace and surfaced in the report's honesty section ("what we
   checked and rejected"), with the exact reason.

`data/samples/hr_attrition_trap.csv` has a planted example: an
`exit_interview_completed` column that's only ever populated *after* an
employee has already left, so a naive analysis finds a near-perfect
correlation with attrition. A Coder script will report r≈0.99. A working
Critic should reject it as leakage rather than let it into the report as
"exit interviews predict attrition." See `data/samples/TRAP_NOTES.md`.

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    ingest[Ingest\nCSV/TSV/XLSX → parquet] --> profiler[Profiler\ndeterministic stats + LLM interpretation]
    profiler --> hyp[Hypothesizer\nfalsifiable claims]
    hyp --> code[Coder\nwrites analysis script]
    code --> exec[Execute\nsandboxed subprocess]
    exec -- exec failed, retries left --> code
    exec -- exec failed, retries exhausted --> advance[Advance\nlog rejection, next hypothesis]
    exec -- success --> critic[Critic\nre-executes independently, judges evidence]
    critic -- revise, retries left --> code
    critic -- revise exhausted / reject --> advance
    critic -- accept --> viz[Visualizer\nnavy/gold chart]
    viz --> advance
    advance -- more hypotheses --> code
    advance -- none left --> report[Report Synthesizer\nfindings + honesty section]
    report --> done([END])
```

Hypotheses are processed **strictly sequentially** — only one Ollama model
fits comfortably in 12GB VRAM at a time, so `app/llm.py` serializes every
call (reasoning and coder models alike) behind a single lock rather than
racing them.

| Agent | Model | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Ingest | — (deterministic) | encoding/delimiter detection, row cap, parquet cache |
| Profiler | `qwen3:14b` | deterministic stats → LLM interpretation, never invents numbers |
| Hypothesizer | `qwen3:14b` | falsifiable, column-grounded hypotheses |
| Coder | `qwen2.5-coder:14b` | writes the analysis script |
| Execute | — (sandbox) | AST security check, subprocess run, `code_hash` |
| Critic | `qwen3:14b`, temp 0.1 | re-executes, judges accept / revise / reject |
| Visualizer | `qwen2.5-coder:14b` | one navy/gold chart per accepted finding |
| Reporter | `qwen3:14b` | findings + honesty section + next steps |

## Prerequisites

- Python 3.11+
- [Ollama](https://ollama.com) running locally with both models pulled:

  ```
  ollama pull qwen3:14b
  ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:14b
  ```

## Quickstart

```
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
copy .env.example .env
python data/samples/generate_samples.py   # writes the 4 demo CSVs
uvicorn app.main:app --reload
```

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 — upload a CSV/TSV/XLSX and watch the live
agent feed; the Report tab populates once the run completes. Click "Open
Trace Viewer" for the full reasoning-chain explorer.

## Config reference (`.env`)

| Var | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `REASONING_MODEL` / `CODER_MODEL` | `qwen3:14b` / `qwen2.5-coder:14b` | Ollama model names |
| `REASONING_TEMPERATURE` / `CODER_TEMPERATURE` | `0.4` / `0.1` | per-role sampling temperature |
| `MODEL_KEEP_ALIVE` | `5m` | how long Ollama keeps a model warm after last use |
| `MAX_HYPOTHESES` | `6` | hypotheses generated per run |
| `MAX_CODER_RETRIES` | `3` | code→execute retries on execution failure |
| `MAX_CRITIC_REJECTIONS` | `2` | critic `revise` round-trips before forcing a reject |
| `EXECUTION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `60` | sandbox subprocess hard timeout |
| `MAX_OUTPUT_CHARS` | `8000` | stdout/stderr truncation |
| `MAX_INGEST_ROWS` | `500000` | row cap on ingested files |
| `MAX_CONCURRENT_RUNS` | `1` | single-GPU concurrency cap; extra uploads queue |

## Trace viewer

`app/static/trace.html?run_id=<id>` is a standalone reasoning-chain
explorer: a collapsible tree (run → hypothesis → coder attempt → execution
→ verdict), a detail panel with the full prompt/output/code/stdout for any
node (syntax-highlighted), a diff view between consecutive coder attempts
for the same hypothesis, agent/type/errors-only filters, a per-agent time
breakdown, and an "Export trace JSON" button. It also accepts a
drag-and-dropped exported JSON file so a trace can be reviewed offline —
useful for sharing with someone who doesn't have the app running.

## Project layout

```text
app/
  main.py, config.py             FastAPI app; env-driven settings
  llm.py                          Ollama JSON-mode client, model-switch lock
  db.py                            SQLite: runs + reports
  models/                           Pydantic v2 schemas, one file per concept
  agents/                            one module per LLM-driven agent
    ingest.py                         deterministic: encoding/delimiter/parquet
    profiler.py, hypothesizer.py,
    coder.py, critic.py, visualizer.py, reporter.py
  execution/
    runner.py                          sandboxed subprocess executor
    ast_security.py                     import/call whitelist+blocklist
  graph/
    state.py, build.py                   LangGraph state + wiring + checkpointing
    execute.py, advance.py                 pure orchestration nodes (no LLM)
  tracing/
    logger.py, storage.py                  trace event tree + SQLite + SSE fan-out
  static/
    index.html, app.js, styles.css          upload UI + live pipeline view
    trace.html                                standalone trace explorer
data/samples/                    demo datasets + generator + trap notes
tests/                            pytest suite (`-m e2e` for live pipeline runs)
workspace/<run_id>/               per-run parquet cache + generated charts
```

## Code contract for generated scripts

Coder and Visualizer scripts run in a subprocess with `df` already loaded
(from the ingested parquet) and `OUTPUT_DIR` predefined. Before execution,
an AST check (`app/execution/ast_security.py`) rejects anything outside a
whitelist of data-analysis imports, plus specific dangerous calls even
within allowed modules (`os.system`, `os.remove`, `eval`, `open`, ...).
Scripts print their result as the last line of stdout, prefixed by a
`###RESULT_JSON###` marker. Matplotlib figures left open at the end of the
script are auto-saved — no `savefig` call needed.

## Tests

```
pytest              # fast: AST security, sandbox, critic (canned LLM responses)
pytest -m e2e        # slow: full pipeline against live Ollama on the demo datasets
```

# QueryPilot
Status: complete
One-liner: A text-to-SQL agent that validates every generated statement at the AST level and gates destructive operations behind human confirmation.

Stack: LangGraph, sqlglot, SQLite, Python
Live URL: https://query-pilot-nine.vercel.app
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/QueryPilot

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
Text-to-SQL safety is usually handled with a regex blocklist for DROP and DELETE, which is security theater — comments, casing, nested statements and string literals all defeat it. QueryPilot parses every generated statement into a sqlglot AST and reasons about what the query structurally does, not what it looks like. Destructive operations don't get blocked outright, because a data tool that can't write is half a tool. They get routed through a LangGraph interrupt that surfaces an FK-aware preview of exactly what a delete would cascade to, and waits for explicit human confirmation. The user keeps the capability and loses the ability to trigger it by accident. Tested against 40 adversarial safety cases — obfuscated destructive queries, injection attempts, multi-statement payloads — with a 100% pass rate. Built against a real dataset from the family cold-drinks distribution business rather than a toy schema, which is where the FK cascade problem showed up in the first place.


## Metrics
- Adversarial safety tests passed: 40/40

## Anticipated questions
Q: Why sqlglot instead of prompting the model to be careful?
A: Prompted safety is a probability, not a guarantee, and it degrades under adversarial input. Parsing gives a deterministic answer to "does this statement delete rows" that doesn't depend on the model cooperating.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)

- Last commit: 2026-09-21T13:28:10Z
- GitHub description: Conversational SQL agent with hard guardrails — natural language → validated SQL via AST inspection, dry-run previews, and confirm-before-write. Fully local (LangGraph + Ollama + SQLite). 60/60 eval accuracy.

## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub)

## README
# QueryPilot

A conversational text-to-SQL agent — ask a database questions in plain
English, or ask it to change something, and watch the agent's own trace as
it validates, previews, and (only after you confirm) executes.

- **Analytics** — ask questions in plain English, get SQL + results + a
  streamed plain-language summary + a chart when the data supports one.
- **Manipulation** — ask for a change (`cancel order 42`, `mark invoice 88
  as paid`), get a preview of exactly which rows would change (including
  FK cascades), and nothing happens until you explicitly confirm.

Every generated SQL statement is deterministically validated (sqlglot AST
inspection, live schema checks, a row-impact ceiling) before it ever
touches the database. **Prompts are not the safety boundary —
`app/core/validator.py` is**, and nothing in later phases (caching,
observability, the LLM provider fallback chain) is allowed to weaken that.

The demo domain is a cold-drinks manufacturing & wholesale distribution
business across Ratnagiri district: products, retailers, orders,
order_items, payments, inventory — ~8,000 orders spanning 2024-2026 with a
real seasonal pattern (summer spike, monsoon dip).

## Live demo

| | |
|---|---|
| Frontend (Vercel) | _add your deployed URL here after following [Deployment](#deployment) below_ |
| Backend (Render) | _add your deployed URL here_ |
| Fallback UI | `<backend URL>/` — `frontend/index.html`, served directly by FastAPI, no build step |

The backend is a Render free-tier instance: it spins down after 15 minutes
idle and takes up to ~1 minute to wake back up on the next request. The
frontend's cold-start gate polls `/health` for up to 90s and shows elapsed
time instead of a broken-looking page — see [Cold starts](#cold-starts).

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    START([user message]) --> GR[guardrail]
    GR -->|blocked, heuristic only, no LLM call| ERR[error_response] --> END0([END])
    GR -->|passed| IC[intent_classifier]
    IC -->|off_topic| PR[polite_redirect] --> END1([END])
    IC -->|schema_question| SQ[schema_question_node] --> END1
    IC -->|analytics / manipulation| SR[schema_retriever]

    SR --> SG[sql_generator]
    SG --> VAL[validator]
    VAL -->|invalid, retries left| SG
    VAL -->|invalid, exhausted| ERR
    VAL -->|valid| AMB[ambiguity_check]

    AMB -->|ambiguous| CQ[ask_clarifying_question] --> END3([END])
    AMB -->|analytics| ALI[auto_limit_injector]
    AMB -->|manipulation| DRP[dry_run_preview]

    ALI --> AE[analytics_executor]
    AE -->|error, retries left| SC[self_corrector] --> AE
    AE -->|error, exhausted| ERR
    AE -->|success| IS[insight_summarizer]
    IS --> CD[chart_detector]
    CD --> FS[followup_suggester]
    FS --> END4([END])

    DRP -->|row-impact ceiling exceeded, or FK-blocked| ERR
    DRP -->|ok| CG["confirmation_gate (LangGraph interrupt)"]
    CG -->|no / timeout| END5([END, cancelled])
    CG -->|yes| TE[transactional_executor]
    TE --> AL[audit_logger] --> END6([END])
```

Every node emits a `node_state` SSE event
(`pending → running → succeeded | degraded | failed | not_reached | skipped_cached`),
so the frontend's center pane renders this exact graph live as a run
executes — including which retry loop fired, which node the validator
rejected SQL at, and which downstream nodes never ran because an earlier
one failed. See [Observability](#observability).

- **Guardrails are code, not prompts.** `app/core/validator.py` whitelists
  statement types, requires a `WHERE` on every write, checks every
  table/column against the *live* schema, and enforces a row-impact
  ceiling via an actual dry-run `COUNT(*)`. `app/core/dry_run.py` rewrites
  `DELETE`/`UPDATE` into `SELECT`s via AST manipulation (not string
  surgery), so the preview's `WHERE` is guaranteed identical to what would
  execute. A heuristic `guardrail` node runs first and catches
  prompt-injection/PII/gibberish patterns with zero LLM cost — but it
  deliberately never pattern-matches SQL keywords, so a message like
  `DROP TABLE orders` sails through it and reaches the validator, which is
  what actually blocks it. This split is intentional: the "Try to break
  it" row in the demo UI shows exactly which layer catches each attack.
- **Schema retrieval is embedding-based**, not a full-schema dump per
  prompt: table descriptions are embedded with Gemini's
  `gemini-embedding-001` and cached to a JSON file keyed by content hash —
  no vector database — and the top-k relevant tables are retrieved per
  request, including live sample rows and explicit enum-value lists for
  low-cardinality columns. If embedding fails for any reason (quota,
  network), it falls back to injecting the full schema (small enough at 6
  tables to be nearly free) and emits a `degraded` node state instead of
  failing the request.
- **The LLM gateway is provider-agnostic and self-healing.** Every node
  asks for an alias (`sql_gen` or `chat`), never a literal model — the
  ordered fallback chain lives in `config/model_groups.yaml`. See
  [Provider fallback](#provider-fallback).
- **Confirmation is a real LangGraph interrupt**, not a fake two-step flow:
  the graph pauses via `interrupt()`, state is checkpointed to SQLite
  (`langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite`), and the API's `/confirm` endpoint
  resumes it with `Command(resume=...)`. A confirmation is scoped to one
  browser session's own sandbox database, never the shared template.

## Provider fallback

Every alias (`sql_gen`, `chat`) has its own ordered chain in
`config/model_groups.yaml`, live-verified against the real provider APIs
(see `docs/phases/01-llm-gateway.md` for the full verification log,
including models that were tried and rejected):

| Order | Provider | `sql_gen` model | `chat` model |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Ollama Cloud | `gpt-oss:120b` | `gpt-oss:20b` |
| 2 | OpenRouter | `cohere/north-mini-code:free` | `nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b:free` |
| 3 | Gemini | `gemini-3.6-flash` | `gemini-3.6-flash` |
| 4 | Groq | `openai/gpt-oss-120b` | `openai/gpt-oss-20b` |

On a timeout, connection error, 5xx, 429, or 401/403/404, the gateway
advances to the next deployment (retrying transient errors once first) and
puts the failing deployment on a 10-minute cooldown. It does **not**
advance on 400/422 (a malformed request fails identically everywhere) or
on a refusal. A deployment-specific bad response — observed live and
documented in `docs/phases/05-evals-ci.md`, where a free-tier OpenRouter
model occasionally returns a response with no `choices` — is classified
and advanced past rather than aborting the whole chain. If every
deployment in a chain fails, the client sees a single honest
`ALL_PROVIDERS_FAILED` error, never a raw exception. `GET
/health/providers` pings every configured deployment live (a real,
billable call — the frontend polls it only on demand, never on a timer).

`QP_LLM_PROFILE=local` forces every alias onto a single local Ollama
deployment instead, for offline development — see [Local
development](#local-development).

**Bring your own key.** `byok_provider` + `byok_api_key` on a `/chat`
request routes that one request through the caller's own key, bypassing
both the shared fallback chain and the daily budget cap. The key is never
logged or persisted, and is redacted from any error text that might echo
it back.

## Observability

Every graph run streams a rich SSE event vocabulary, all consumed live by
the frontend's center (trace) and right (results) panes:

- `node_state` — `pending → running → succeeded | degraded | failed | not_reached | skipped_cached`, one per node, computed straight from LangGraph's own task-start/task-end stream (not inferred).
- `guardrail`, `validator_verdict` — the heuristic guardrail's verdict, and a structured list of which validator checks ran and passed (statement type, tables/columns exist, WHERE-clause required, auto-LIMIT injected, row-impact within ceiling).
- `llm_attempt`, `cache_hit` — provider, model, latency, tokens, cost per attempt; forwarded live from the same events `app/core/budget.py` uses to track spend.
- `sql_generated`, `preview`, `awaiting_confirmation`, `result`, `chart`, `followups`, `token` (streamed insight text) — the existing per-node semantic payloads.
- `error` — `{code, message, node}` from the taxonomy below, never a raw exception.
- `heartbeat` — every 15 seconds, so a slow multi-provider fallback chain (observed live at 30-250+ seconds in a worst case) never looks like a dead connection.
- `done` — a per-run summary: total latency, per-node latency, LLM attempts by provider, tokens, cost, cache savings, and (if Langfuse is configured) a trace URL.

**Error taxonomy** (`app/core/errors.py`): every error crossing the API
boundary is `{code, message, node}` — `PROVIDER_TIMEOUT`,
`PROVIDER_RATE_LIMIT`, `PROVIDER_AUTH_FAILED`, `PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE`,
`ALL_PROVIDERS_FAILED`, `GUARDRAIL_BLOCKED`, `VALIDATION_BLOCKED`,
`ROW_CEILING_EXCEEDED`, `FK_BLOCKED`, `SCHEMA_VALIDATION_FAILED`,
`SESSION_EXPIRED`, `SESSION_INVALID`, `RATE_LIMITED`, `BUDGET_EXCEEDED`,
`INTERNAL`. Every one of these has a designed UI state in the frontend
(a message plus a next action — retry, reset sandbox, add your own key,
wait for the rate limit) — never a blank screen or raw exception text.

**Optional Langfuse tracing** activates automatically when
`LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY`/`LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY` are set: one trace per `/chat`
or `/confirm` call, one span per node, one generation per LLM attempt. A
Langfuse outage or missing keys never breaks a request either way.

## Frontend

`web/` is a Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind 4) app, deployed
to Vercel with `web/` as the project root. It talks to the backend
**directly** — `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL`, no Next.js API routes, no
proxying of the SSE stream through a serverless function. `frontend/
index.html` is kept as a lightweight, build-step-free fallback UI served
directly by FastAPI.

Three panes:

- **Sandbox & context** (left) — a session card (your own isolated
  sandbox database, with a reset button), a table browser with a
  paginated preview modal, example prompts split into analytics/
  manipulation, a **"Try to break it"** row of preset attacks (`DROP TABLE
  orders`, "delete all orders", a prompt-injection attempt, "update every
  retailer's credit limit to 0") that each show live which layer blocks
  them, provider status dots, a budget meter, and a bring-your-own-key
  form (shown automatically once the budget is exceeded).
- **Live agent trace** (center) — the graph above, rendered as a vertical
  pipeline with live `node_state` styling; retries, self-correction loops,
  and validator rejections are all visible as they happen, each node
  showing its latency and which provider answered.
- **Results** (right) — syntax-highlighted generated SQL with validator-
  check badges, a results table, a chart, the streamed insight, clickable
  follow-up suggestions, a preview card for writes (exact rows, FK
  cascade preview, confirm/cancel with a live countdown matching
  `QP_CONFIRMATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`), an audit tab, and a run summary.

Design tokens (the dark, restrained teal/amber/coral "control-room
telemetry" palette, and the `NodeState` styling) are shared with the
sibling `Crewai-Research-pipeline` project's dashboard.

## Guardrails (all code, not prompts)

1. Statement whitelist: only `SELECT`/`INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`; everything
   else (`DROP`, `TRUNCATE`, `ALTER`, `CREATE`, `GRANT`, `PRAGMA`,
   `ATTACH`, `VACUUM`, ...) is rejected by AST node type, not keyword
   matching.
2. Single statement only — multi-statement input (`;`-separated, including
   classic injection payloads) is rejected.
3. `WHERE` required on every `DELETE`/`UPDATE`.
4. Every referenced table/column is checked against the *live* schema
   (`PRAGMA table_info`), catching hallucinated references.
5. Row-impact ceiling (default 50): a real dry-run `COUNT(*)` against the
   write's actual `WHERE` clause; anything over the limit is blocked
   before the user ever sees a confirmation prompt. For `DELETE`, this
   walks the live foreign-key graph too — cascade-deleted rows in other
   tables count toward the ceiling, not just the target table.
6. Auto-`LIMIT` on analytics `SELECT`s that lack one.
7. Read-only enforcement at the SQLite driver level (`mode=ro` URI) — a
   validator bug cannot result in a write on the analytics path, because
   the connection itself is incapable of writing.
8. `EXPLAIN` pre-flight before every real execution.
9. Transactions: `BEGIN` → execute → `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK` on any error.
10. Every manipulation request logged to the operational database
    (Neon Postgres in production, a local SQLite file otherwise) via
    `app/core/audit.py`: timestamp, input, SQL, validation outcome,
    preview, confirmed/cancelled, rows affected, latency, retry count.
11. `QP_READ_ONLY_MODE=true` disables the manipulation path entirely.
12. **Foreign-key-aware deletes.** `orders → order_items` and
    `orders → payments` are `ON DELETE CASCADE`, so
    `validator.check_row_impact` walks `PRAGMA foreign_key_list` on every
    table: rows in `ON DELETE CASCADE` children are *shown in the preview*
    and counted toward the row-impact ceiling; rows in children *without*
    a cascade path (e.g. `order_items.product_id`, `orders.retailer_id` —
    deliberately not cascaded, so deleting a product or retailer never
    silently wipes historical order data) **block the delete outright**
    with a clear reason, before the user ever sees a confirmation prompt.
13. **A heuristic input guardrail** runs before any LLM call: message
    length, a gibberish-symbol-ratio check, prompt-injection/role-override
    phrase patterns, and PII patterns (email, SSN-shaped, credit-card-
    shaped digit runs). Zero LLM cost on a block. Deliberately does *not*
    pattern-match SQL keywords — see [Architecture](#architecture) above.
14. **Per-session sandboxing.** Every visitor gets their own SQLite copy
    of the seeded template database; the analytics/manipulation guardrails
    above all introspect that session's own live schema, never a shared
    one two visitors could race on.
15. **A per-IP rate limit** (`QP_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE`, default 10) and a
    **daily USD budget cap** (`QP_DAILY_BUDGET_USD`) on top of everything
    above — both bypassable per-request only via BYOK.

`tests/test_guardrails.py` (40 tests) and `tests/test_guardrail_input.py`
cover the adversarial set: `DROP TABLE`, `'; DROP TABLE products; --`,
DELETE/UPDATE without `WHERE`, queries against nonexistent tables/columns,
>50-row writes, the cascade/foreign-key cases above, and the heuristic
guardrail's own block/pass cases. All 279 backend tests pass (excluding 3
tests in `test_schema_embeddings.py` that make real, occasionally
quota-limited Gemini API calls — documented in-file as expected).

## Evals

`python -m evals.run_evals` runs 68 hand-written cases (10 simple selects,
10 joins, 10 aggregations, 10 time/seasonal, 5 follow-up/context, 10
manipulation commands, 8 guardrail cases, 5 deliberately ambiguous
requests) through the real agent graph — same code path as production —
using the Phase 1 cloud gateway and a fresh per-session sandbox database
per case, so a manipulation case's real commit can never contaminate
another case or the shared template. It measures **execution accuracy**
(does the agent's SQL return the same data as a hand-written reference
query, tolerating extra helpful columns, not string-matching SQL text)
and **guardrail correctness** (does the heuristic block what it should and
let through what it shouldn't) separately, each with a 95% bootstrap
confidence interval, plus p50/p95 latency.

### Latest scorecard (2026-09-21, live cloud run)

| Category | Passed | Accuracy | 95% CI |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| aggregation | 10/10 | 100.0% | [100.0%, 100.0%] |
| ambiguous | 5/5 | 100.0% | [100.0%, 100.0%] |
| followup | 4/5 | 80.0% | [40.0%, 100.0%] |
| guardrail | 8/8 | 100.0% | [100.0%, 100.0%] |
| join | 10/10 | 100.0% | [100.0%, 100.0%] |
| manipulation | 8/10 | 80.0% | [50.0%, 100.0%] |
| simple_select | 10/10 | 100.0% | [100.0%, 100.0%] |
| time_based | 9/10 | 90.0% | [70.0%, 100.0%] |
| **Execution accuracy** (all non-guardrail categories) | | **93.3%** | |
| **Guardrail correctness** | | **100.0%** | |

Latency: mean 35.9s, p50 20.6s, p95 131.1s per case — this run happened
while the Gemini free-tier embedding quota was fully exhausted for the
day, so every case paid a real retry-then-fallback penalty on `
schema_retriever` before degrading gracefully to the full schema; not a
clean steady-state number (documented in `docs/phases/05-evals-ci.md`).
The old **local-Ollama baseline** (60 cases, pre-cloud-gateway,
`evals/eval_results.local_ollama_baseline.json`) scored 100% with a mean
latency of 49.4s/case (max 835.9s) — the two aren't directly comparable
(different case sets, different infra), but p50 latency on the cloud
stack is faster despite everything above.

Every one of the 4 individual case failures in the latest run was traced
to a specific, understood cause, not left as an unexplained number — see
`docs/phases/05-evals-ci.md` for the full breakdown: one real
infrastructure rate-limit exhaustion (all 4 providers failed on one
call), one genuine multi-turn context miss by the model (a follow-up lost
the prior turn's "top 3 by revenue" ranking), and two cases of
`ambiguity_check` non-deterministically — and arguably reasonably —
asking about cascade-delete behavior before a destructive `DELETE`.

**`.github/workflows/eval.yml`** runs this suite on every push to `main`,
committing `evals/eval_results.json`/`evals/SUMMARY.md` back to the repo
and failing the job if guardrail correctness drops below 100% or
execution accuracy drops more than 5 points below the last committed run.

## Memory and latency

Measured on a fresh `docker build` of the exact image Render deploys
(`python:3.11-slim` base, no unusual dependencies), on 2026-09-21:

- **Image size**: 607MB (up from 581MB in Phase 2d — Phase 4's Langfuse +
  OpenTelemetry dependencies).
- **Idle RSS** (container up, before any request): ~133MiB.
- **Peak RSS under a real manipulation flow** (`docker run` the built
  image, real cloud providers end to end: guardrail → ... → confirmation
  → commit → audit): **152.6MiB**, about 30% of Render free tier's 512MB
  limit — see `docs/phases/07-docs-and-deployment.md` for the full sample
  sequence. Headroom for concurrent sessions is ample (each session's
  sandbox is a small SQLite file copy; the bulk of resident memory is the
  shared Python process, FastAPI/Uvicorn, and the loaded LLM/embedding/
  tracing client libraries).

## Deployment

Three free-tier services: **Render** (backend), **Vercel** (frontend),
**Neon** (Postgres — audit events and budget entries only; LangGraph
checkpoints and per-session sandboxes stay in ephemeral local SQLite,
which is fine to lose on a spin-down).

### 1. Neon (Postgres)

1. Create a free project at [neon.tech](https://neon.tech).
2. Copy the connection string from the dashboard (the bare
   `postgresql://...` string — QueryPilot normalizes it to the psycopg3
   dialect automatically). Keep it for step 2's `QP_DATABASE_URL`.
3. Nothing else to do here — `alembic upgrade head` (run automatically by
   the Docker image's `CMD`) creates `audit_events` and `budget_entries`
   on first deploy.

### 2. Render (backend)

1. Push this repo to GitHub (or your own fork).
2. In the Render dashboard: **New → Blueprint**, point it at the repo.
   Render reads `render.yaml` and creates a free-tier Docker web service
   (`querypilot-backend`) with every env var already declared — the ones
   marked `sync: false` need their values filled in:
   - `QP_DATABASE_URL` — the Neon connection string from step 1.
   - `QP_ADMIN_TOKEN` — any random string, for the `/audit` full-log admin
     view (optional; leave blank to disable it).
   - `QP_CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` — leave blank for now, come back after step
     3 gives you the Vercel URL.
   - `OLLAMA_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`,
     `GROQ_API_KEY` — see [Local development](#local-development) for
     where to get each one. At minimum, one working provider per alias is
     enough for the fallback chain to function.
   - Optional: `LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY`/`LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY` (tracing).
3. Deploy. Render builds the Docker image (`Dockerfile`), which seeds
   `data/template.db` at build time, then the container's `CMD` runs
   `alembic upgrade head` before starting `uvicorn`. Health check path is
   `/health`.
4. Note the deployed URL (`https://<service>.onrender.com`) — this is
   `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` for step 3.

### 3. Vercel (frontend)

1. In the Vercel dashboard: **New Project**, import the same repo, and
   set **Root Directory** to `web/`.
2. Add one environment variable: `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` = the Render
   URL from step 2 (no trailing slash).
3. Deploy (Vercel auto-detects Next.js — no build config needed).
4. Go back to Render and set `QP_CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` to the deployed
   Vercel URL (comma-separated if you also want to allow a preview
   domain), then redeploy the backend so the new CORS origin takes
   effect.
5. Open the Vercel URL. The cold-start gate will show "Waking up the
   backend…" for up to a minute if Render's instance was idle — see
   [Cold starts](#cold-starts).

### Cold starts

Render's free tier spins down a web service after **15 minutes** of no
inbound traffic and takes **up to ~1 minute** to cold-start the next
request. The frontend's `Dashboard` component polls `GET /health` (with a
90-second timeout) before rendering the three-pane app, showing an
explicit "Waking up the backend…" message with elapsed time instead of a
blank or broken-looking page. If the backend is already warm, this gate
is invisible (one fast `/health` call, then straight to the app).

fallback if you'd rather stay fully offline.




Runs against a real locally-started backend for every fast/no-LLM
endpoint, with `/chat`/`/confirm`'s SSE streams intercepted by canned,
deterministic fixtures (`web/tests/fixtures/sse.ts`) — real provider
latency isn't part of this suite; that's what `evals/run_evals.py` is for.

## Using your own database

QueryPilot ships seeded with a synthetic cold-drinks distribution dataset
(`scripts/seed_db.py`) so the demo works out of the box, but nothing in the
agent, validator, or schema retrieval is hardcoded to that domain — swap in
your own SQLite database and it adapts automatically.

1. **Point `QP_TEMPLATE_DB_PATH` at your file**, or drop it in as
   `data/template.db` (the default path).
2. **Enable foreign keys, if your schema has them** — `app/core/db.py`
   already turns `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON` for every connection; just make
   sure your schema actually declares `REFERENCES parent(id)`, not just
   implicit joins by convention, for the FK-cascade guardrail to work.
3. **(Optional) Clear the stale schema embeddings cache** if you're
   replacing a table with the same name and a different shape:
   `rm data/schema_embeddings.json` (rebuilt automatically on next use).
4. **(Optional but recommended) Add business-purpose descriptions** —
   `TABLE_PURPOSES` in `app/core/schema_store.py`, a hand-written
   `{table_name: "what this table is for"}` dict that helps retrieval for
   ambiguous table names. Columns/types/sample values are always
   introspected live regardless.
5. **Restart the app.**

## Configuration reference

All `QP_`-prefixed vars are read by `app/config.py`'s `Settings`; provider
credentials (`OLLAMA_API_KEY`, `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`,
`GROQ_API_KEY`) and `LANGFUSE_*` are unprefixed on purpose, matching
Render's blueprint. Full list with explanations in `.env.example`;
highlights:

| Variable | Default | What it controls |
|---|---|---|
| `QP_READ_ONLY_MODE` | `false` | Disables the manipulation path entirely |
| `QP_ROW_IMPACT_CEILING` | `50` | Max rows a write may affect (incl. cascades) |
| `QP_AUTO_LIMIT` | `200` | LIMIT injected into SELECTs that lack one |
| `QP_CONFIRMATION_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` | `60` | Interrupt window for `/confirm` |
| `QP_SESSION_TTL_MINUTES` / `QP_MAX_SESSIONS` | `30` / `200` | Per-session sandbox lifecycle |
| `QP_LLM_PROFILE` | `cloud` | `cloud` (fallback chain) or `local` (offline dev) |
| `QP_LLM_CACHE_ENABLED` | `true` | Exact-match cache for intent/SQL generation |
| `QP_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE` | `10` | Per-IP sliding window on `/chat`, `/confirm` |
| `QP_DAILY_BUDGET_USD` | `0.0` (no cap) | Daily spend kill-switch, bypassable via BYOK |
| `QP_DATABASE_URL` | unset (local SQLite) | Neon Postgres connection string |
| `QP_ADMIN_TOKEN` | unset | `X-Admin-Token` for the full (all-sessions) `/audit` log |
| `QP_CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS` | unset (blocks all) | Comma-separated allowed origins |
| `LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY`/`SECRET_KEY`/`HOST` | unset (disabled) | Optional tracing |
