# DocIntel
Status: complete
One-liner: OCR-free extraction from Indian financial documents using a fine-tuned Donut model, with a learned router deciding when to use it.

Stack: Donut, PyTorch, LightGBM, Python
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/DocIntel

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
The premise was that an OCR-free vision-language model would beat a traditional OCR pipeline on Indian invoices, where layout variance and multilingual text break conventional extraction. It didn't — the fine-tuned Donut model scored 51.0% against the OCR baseline's 63.6% overall. The result underneath that headline is more useful: Donut wins specifically on free-text fields, where OCR's line-segmentation assumptions fall apart, and loses on structured numeric fields where OCR is nearly exact. So rather than picking a winner, the system routes per-field with a LightGBM classifier, using each approach where it's actually stronger. Trained on real invoice data from the family business, and kept at ~683ms p50 latency so it's viable in a document-processing pipeline rather than just a notebook result.


## Metrics
- Donut accuracy (overall): 51.0%
- OCR baseline (overall): 63.6%
- p50 latency: ~683ms

## Anticipated questions
Q: Your fine-tuned model lost to the baseline. Why is this on your portfolio?
A: Because the honest version of the result is the useful one. The interesting finding wasn't "Donut is better" — it was that the two approaches fail on disjoint field types, which is what makes routing between them worth building. A portfolio that only contains wins is a portfolio where the negative results got buried.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)
- Stars: 0
- Last commit: 2026-08-07T14:49:22Z
- GitHub description: Multimodal document intelligence for Indian financial documents (GST invoices, receipts, bank statements) — Donut-based OCR-free extraction, synthetic data generation, fraud/anomaly detection, and FastAPI serving

## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub)
- Jupyter Notebook: 2581071
- Python: 467891
- Jinja: 12055
- Dockerfile: 2096
- Mako: 635

## README
# DocIntel

A production-grade multimodal document intelligence system for Indian financial
documents (GST invoices, receipts, bank statements, salary slips). Extracts
structured fields from document images using a fine-tuned Donut model
(OCR-free vision-encoder-decoder), classifies document types, and flags
anomalies/fraud using classical ML.

See [CLAUDE.md](CLAUDE.md) for the full spec, stack, and target schema.

## Progress

| Phase | Status | Summary |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Synthetic data generator | ✅ Done | Faker + Jinja2 + Playwright + Albumentations pipeline generating labeled invoices/receipts at scale |
| 2. Annotation + dataset builders | ✅ Done | Label Studio setup, export/import converters, Donut/LayoutLM dataset builders, leakage-safe splits |
| 3. OCR + heuristics baseline | ✅ Done | PaddleOCR/Tesseract baseline extractor + shared eval metrics (exact match, edit distance, Hungarian line-item matching) |
| 4. Donut fine-tuning | ✅ Trained | Fine-tuned end-to-end on an RTX 5070 (20 epochs, 533 synthetic docs). Real result on a 67-doc held-out val split: 51.0% mean field accuracy vs. 63.6% for the OCR+heuristics baseline — Donut wins on free-text fields (date, invoice_no, vendor_name) but trails on rigid structured codes like GSTIN; see PHASE_NOTES.md for the full per-field breakdown and why |
| 5. Document classification + anomaly detection | ✅ Done | LightGBM/MobileNetV3 doc classifier (5-fold CV, macro-F1 1.000/0.992), rule-engine + Isolation Forest + SHAP fraud detector (precision@10%=75.0%), 6-type anomaly-injection benchmark |
| 6. Robustness + confidence routing | ✅ Done | Degradation curves (blur/rotation/downscale), calibration (ECE) + confidence-based review routing (+13.3pp accuracy lift @30% budget), end-to-end integration test, `full_report` CLI |
| 7. Serving (FastAPI) | 🟡 Built, Docker unverified | ONNX export (encoder + decoder-with-past-KV, fp16/int8) + benchmark (int8 3.3x faster than PyTorch on CPU); FastAPI app (extract/batch/jobs/review/health/metrics) + async Postgres/SQLAlchemy + Alembic, tested against SQLite; Dockerfile/compose written but not build-verified (no Docker daemon in this sandbox) — see PHASE_NOTES.md |
| 8. Monitoring + retraining loop | ✅ Done | Drift detection (KS-test on brightness/blur/confidence/anomaly score), Chart.js dashboard at `/dashboard`, review-driven retraining with regression-gated promotion (reuses Phase 4's training loop) — see [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md) for the full closed loop |

Decisions and notes for each phase are in [PHASE_NOTES.md](PHASE_NOTES.md). The complete
ingestion → extraction → confidence routing → human review → retraining → promotion loop, with a
diagram, is in [ARCHITECTURE.md](ARCHITECTURE.md).

## Setup

```bash
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate            # Windows
pip install -e ".[dev]"
playwright install chromium       # needed by the synthetic data generator
pre-commit install
```

**Note on the dependency set**: `paddleocr==2.9.1` and `albumentations` pin to
exact transitive versions of each other's dependencies (`albumentations==1.4.10`,
`albucore==0.0.13`, `protobuf==3.20.2` to match `paddlepaddle`, and both
`opencv-contrib-python`/`opencv-python` since paddleocr requires both). These
pins were resolved empirically (see `pip check`) rather than picking the
newest version of each package independently, because paddleocr forces the
older versions transitively. See PHASE_NOTES.md for the full story.

**Note on Windows + native libraries**: PaddlePaddle and PyTorch have a native
DLL conflict in the same process on Windows (paddle-first breaks torch's DLL
loader). `tests/conftest.py` forces `import torch` before any test module can
trigger a `paddleocr` import to avoid this — if you write a standalone script
that uses both, import `torch` first.

## Running things

```bash
# Phase 1: generate synthetic invoices/receipts
python -m docintel.data.synthetic --count 1000 --severity mixed --out data/synthetic/

# Phase 2: annotation (optional, for real scans)
docker compose -f docker-compose.annotation.yml up -d
# then import configs/labelstudio_interface.xml as the project's labeling config

# Phase 2: assign train/val/test splits across synthetic + real manifests
python -m docintel.data.splits --synthetic-manifest data/synthetic/manifest.parquet --out data/splits/splits.parquet

# Phase 3: run the OCR+heuristics baseline over a split and score it
# (--split val, not test -- see the Phase 4 note below on why "test" is empty
# in a synthetic-only project state)
python -m docintel.eval.run --model baseline --split val --data-root data/synthetic

# Phase 4: fine-tune Donut (needs a real GPU -- ~85 min for 20 epochs on 533 docs on an RTX 5070)
python -m docintel.training.train_donut --config configs/train_donut.yaml

# Phase 4: evaluate a Donut checkpoint with the same report format as the baseline
# (note: --split val, not test -- the "test" split is reserved for real
# annotation-QA'd documents per configs/splits.yaml and is empty in a
# synthetic-only project state)
python -m docintel.eval.run --model donut --checkpoint checkpoints/donut/stage1_synthetic/epoch_017 --split val --data-root data/synthetic

# Phase 5: cross-validate the document-type classifiers (LightGBM + MobileNetV3)
python -m docintel.models.doc_classifier --manifest data/synthetic/manifest.parquet --data-root data/synthetic --backend both

# Phase 5: build the labeled anomaly benchmark, then fit + evaluate the fraud detector
python -m docintel.data.inject_anomalies --manifest data/synthetic/manifest.parquet --data-root data/synthetic --out data/anomaly_benchmark
python -m docintel.models.anomaly --benchmark data/anomaly_benchmark/manifest.parquet --data-root data/anomaly_benchmark

# Phase 6: controlled-degradation robustness curves + confidence calibration/routing
python -m docintel.eval.robustness --model baseline --manifest data/synthetic/manifest.parquet --data-root data/synthetic
python -m docintel.eval.confidence --model baseline --manifest data/synthetic/manifest.parquet --data-root data/synthetic

# Phase 6: run (or assemble results from) every evaluation stage into one report
python -m docintel.eval.full_report --run all

# Phase 7: export Donut to ONNX (encoder + decoder-with-past-KV, fp16/int8) and benchmark vs. PyTorch
python -m docintel.serving.export --checkpoint naver-clova-ix/donut-base --stage all

# Phase 8: compare a recent window of ingested documents against a reference window for drift
python -m docintel.monitoring.drift

# Phase 8: fine-tune on human-reviewed corrections; promotes only if field-accuracy doesn't regress
python -m docintel.training.retrain --config configs/retrain.yaml
```

## Repo layout

```text
src/docintel/
  data/        synthetic generator, augmentation, Label Studio I/O, dataset builders, splits,
               inject_anomalies.py (6-type anomaly-injection benchmark generator)
  models/      baseline.py (OCR + heuristics), donut_infer.py (Donut generation + parsing),
               doc_classifier.py (LightGBM/MobileNetV3), anomaly.py (rule engine + Isolation Forest + SHAP)
  eval/        shared metrics + docintel.eval.run (extraction), robustness.py (degradation curves),
               confidence.py (calibration + review routing), full_report.py (assembles everything)
  training/    train_donut.py (fine-tuning loop, VRAM guard, curriculum, checkpointing),
               retrain.py (human-review retraining loop, regression-gated promotion)
  serving/     export.py (ONNX export + fp16/int8 + PyTorch-vs-ONNX benchmark), db.py (async
               SQLAlchemy models), app.py (FastAPI: extract/batch/jobs/review/health/metrics),
               train_artifacts.py (fits + joblib-persists the doc classifier + anomaly detector app.py loads)
  monitoring/  drift.py (rolling KS-test drift detection), dashboard.py (Chart.js dashboard,
               served at /dashboard from app.py)
configs/       YAML config for every module above (pydantic-settings backed)
data/          raw/ synthetic/ annotated/ splits/ anomaly_benchmark/ (all gitignored except .gitkeep / vendor & catalog data)
notebooks/     sanity-check + analysis notebooks per phase
tests/         mirrors src/, one test module per source module
results/       eval CLI output (parquet + markdown reports + plots), FULL_REPORT.md
```

## Serving

```bash
# Local dev: fit + persist the artifacts app.py loads at startup, then run it
# against a local Postgres (docker compose up -d postgres, or any Postgres URL)
python -m docintel.serving.train_artifacts
alembic upgrade head
uvicorn docintel.serving.app:app --reload

# Everything in containers (CPU variant is the default compose target -- runs
# anywhere, no GPU needed; pass `target: gpu` in docker-compose.yml's `build`
# section for the RTX 5070 host)
docker compose up --build
```

`configs/serving.yaml` defaults `extractor_model: baseline` (no trained Donut checkpoint exists
yet -- see PHASE_NOTES.md, Phase 4); set it to `donut` + a `donut_checkpoint` path once one does,
no code changes needed. A fresh deployment with no `checkpoints/serving/*.joblib` artifacts still
serves `/extract` — it just returns `doc_type: null` / `anomaly_score: null` instead of failing to
start.

### Load testing

```bash
pip install -e ".[dev]"          # includes locust
docker compose up --build -d     # or run `uvicorn docintel.serving.app:app` directly
locust -f locustfile.py --host http://localhost:8000
```

Then open `http://localhost:8089`, set the number of users / spawn rate, and start the test.
`locustfile.py`'s `DocIntelUser` exercises `/extract`, `/batch` + `/jobs/{id}` polling, and
`/health` at a 5:2:1 ratio.

## Tests

```bash
pytest
ruff check src tests
mypy src/docintel
```

A few tests are skipped automatically when their runtime dependency isn't
available in the current environment (Playwright's Chromium browser, a
working PaddleOCR/Tesseract install, or network access to download the
`naver-clova-ix/donut-base` processor from the Hugging Face Hub).

documents.content:
# MarathiGPT
Status: complete
One-liner: A 54M-parameter GPT pretrained from scratch on Marathi with a custom tokenizer that's 4.8x more token-efficient than GPT-4 on the language.

Stack: PyTorch, SentencePiece, transformer pretraining
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/Marathi-GPT

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
For Indic languages the binding constraint usually isn't model capacity, it's tokenization. GPT-4's tokenizer shreds Devanagari into fragments, so the same Marathi sentence costs several times more tokens than its English equivalent — which means worse context utilization, higher inference cost, and less semantic signal per token during training. So the project started at the tokenizer: a custom 32k SentencePiece vocabulary trained on Marathi, achieving 4.8x better token efficiency than GPT-4 on the same text. The transformer was then pretrained from scratch on top of it, at 54M parameters, with 22.9M (nano) and 42.1M (small) variants to see how the efficiency gain interacts with scale. Small models by design — the point was to demonstrate the tokenizer thesis end-to-end on a single consumer GPU, not to compete with anything.


## Metrics
- Token efficiency vs GPT-4 on Marathi: 4.8x
- Model sizes trained: 22.9M / 42.1M / 54M

## Anticipated questions
Q: Why build the tokenizer instead of fine-tuning an existing model?
A: Fine-tuning inherits the tokenizer, and the tokenizer is the actual bottleneck. You can't fine-tune your way out of spending 5x the tokens to say the same sentence.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)
- Stars: 0
- Last commit: 2026-08-07T13:10:04Z
- GitHub description: GPT pretrained from scratch on Marathi — custom 32k SentencePiece tokenizer (4.8x fewer tokens than GPT-4's on Marathi), full corpus → cleaning → tokenizer → training → eval pipeline, trained on a single RTX 5070 (12GB)

## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub)
- Python: 123941

## README
# MarathiGPT

A GPT-style language model pretrained from scratch on Marathi text, nanoGPT-style
(architecture + training loop written from first principles, no fine-tuned base model).

Portfolio project: full pretraining stack — corpus collection, cleaning, a custom
tokenizer, model, training loop, and evaluation — for a low-resource Indian language,
trained on a single consumer GPU (RTX 5070, 12GB).

See [marathi-gpt-project-plan.md](marathi-gpt-project-plan.md) for the full blueprint.

## Status

Work in progress. Built phase by phase:

- [x] Phase 1 — Repo scaffold
- [x] Phase 2 — Data download
- [x] Phase 3 — Cleaning pipeline
- [x] Phase 4 — Tokenizer
- [x] Phase 5 — Pre-tokenization
- [x] Phase 6 — Model
- [x] Phase 7 — Training loop
- [x] Phase 8 — Sampling & eval
- [x] Phase 9 — SFT + demo

## Repo structure

```
marathi-gpt/
├── configs/            # nano / small / base model + training configs
├── data/               # download, clean, tokenizer training, pre-tokenization
├── model.py            # ~300-line decoder-only transformer
├── train.py            # single-file training loop
├── sample.py           # generation from checkpoints
├── eval/               # perplexity, few-shot sentiment, tokenizer fertility
├── sft/                # instruction-tuning data + fine-tuning
└── app/                # Gradio chat demo
```

## Setup

```bash
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate      # Windows
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128  # CUDA build; verified on RTX 5070
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## Quickstart

```bash
python data/download.py --source wikipedia --limit 1000   # drop --limit for the full source
python data/clean.py --limit 1000
python data/train_tokenizer.py --limit 1000 --vocab-size 1000  # drop both for a real 32k tokenizer
python data/prepare.py --limit 1000
python train.py --config configs/nano.yaml --benchmark     # pure throughput/MFU check, no data needed
python train.py --config configs/nano.yaml --max-steps 500 # a real (if small) training run
python sample.py --checkpoint checkpoints/nano/best.pt      # generate from prompts/gallery_mr.txt
python eval/perplexity.py --checkpoint checkpoints/nano/best.pt
python eval/mahasent_fewshot.py --checkpoint checkpoints/nano/best.pt --limit 300
python sft/build_instruct_data.py                           # pulls Marathi Dolly from ai4bharat/indic-align
python sft/finetune.py --checkpoint checkpoints/nano/best.pt --checkpoint-dir checkpoints/sft-nano
python app/gradio_demo.py --checkpoint checkpoints/sft-nano/best.pt
```

### First real training run

Ran the full pipeline end-to-end on the complete Marathi Wikipedia (94,133
articles) rather than a toy sample: `download.py --source wikipedia` (no
limit) → `clean.py` (54,895 docs survived langID/quality/dedup) →
`train_tokenizer.py --vocab-size 32000` (real 32k-vocab tokenizer, see
`assets/fertility_chart.png` — 4.8x fewer tokens than GPT-4's cl100k_base on
held-out Marathi) → `prepare.py` (33.1M train tokens after Wikipedia's 2x
upweight) → `train.py --config configs/nano.yaml --max-steps 500`.

Nano (22.9M params) trained in ~28 minutes on the RTX 5070: loss went
8.63 → 4.39 (train) / 4.59 (val) over 500 steps (262M tokens). Sample
generation at that checkpoint produces grammatical Marathi with correctly-
learned Wikipedia article structure (section headers like "इतिहास"/History,
"बाह्य दुवे"/External links) but falls into repetition loops on longer
continuations - expected for a 22.9M-param model this early in training, not
a bug.

Small (42.1M params) trained on the identical data/token budget (500 steps,
262M tokens) in ~89 minutes: loss went 8.69 → 4.25 (train) / 4.56 (val) -
modestly better than nano at the same budget, as expected for more params.
Its generations are noticeably more fluent: full, grammatically clean
sentences ("पुणे शहर हे येथील ऐतिहासिक शहर होते" - "Pune city was a historic
city here") and a correctly-reproduced Wikipedia city-article template
(इतिहास/History, भूगोल/Geography, हवामान/Climate, लोकसंख्या/Population
sections with plausible census-style demographic prose). One prompt still
degenerated into a nonsense numeral sequence - a real, honest failure mode at
this scale/budget, not cherry-picked away.

### Evaluation (Phase 8)

`eval/perplexity.py` walks the held-out splits exhaustively (non-overlapping
block_size chunks, not a sampled estimate) and reports perplexity separately
per split. On the small model:

| Split | Tokens | Loss | Perplexity |
|-------|--------|------|------------|
| val | 72,704 | 4.5596 | 95.55 |
| wiki_val | 388,096 | 4.6273 | 102.23 |

`eval/mahasent_fewshot.py` runs 3-shot sentiment classification on
[L3Cube MahaSent](https://github.com/l3cube-pune/MarathiNLP) (Marathi tweets,
3-class) by scoring label-word log-likelihoods - no fine-tuning, the model
just picks whichever label continuation it finds most probable. On 300 held-out
test tweets: **33.7% accuracy** (101/300) vs a 33.3% random baseline -
chance level. Expected and honest: the model has only ever seen Wikipedia
prose, never tweets or social-register text, and 42M params / 262M
pretraining tokens isn't enough to generalize zero-shot to an unseen domain
and label-verbalizer task. A real result, not swept under the rug.

### Instruction tuning & demo (Phase 9)

`sft/build_instruct_data.py` builds the SFT set from
[ai4bharat/indic-align](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai4bharat/indic-align)'s
Marathi-translated Dolly split (IndicTrans2-translated by AI4Bharat) plus 18
hand-written examples in `sft/manual_examples.jsonl` (greetings, Marathi
proverbs, basic facts) - **14,950 train / 79 val** examples after holding out
examples longer than the model's context. (Anudesh, a second candidate
source, turned out to have an undocumented, non-parallel schema on inspection
- English-only `interactions` with no per-language columns - so it was left
out rather than risk silently training on English text; see the comment in
`build_instruct_data.py`.)

`sft/finetune.py` does a full fine-tune (42M params is small enough that
LoRA isn't necessary) of the small pretrained checkpoint, with the loss
masked to the assistant's response tokens only (not the `<|user|>` prompt).
2,796 steps (3 epochs, micro-batch 16, lr 2e-5 cosine) took **~8 minutes** on
the RTX 5070: val loss went 5.37 → **4.90**. Sample chat turns after SFT:

```
USER: नमस्कार, तू कोण आहेस?
ASSISTANT: मला मला सर्वात चांगले वाटते. मला वाटते की मला एक वाईट मत आहे...
  (grammatical Marathi, but repetitive and doesn't actually answer - typical
  small-model/small-SFT-budget failure mode)

USER: महाराष्ट्राची राजधानी कोणती आहे?
ASSISTANT: महाराष्ट्र
  (on-topic but incomplete/wrong - should be "मुंबई")

USER: एक छोटी मराठी कविता लिही.
ASSISTANT: सुरुवातीला, 'अ' हा सर्व कविता सादर करण्यासाठी, 'धाक्या' हा एक उत्तम
कथा दिग्दर्शन आणि दिग्दर्शन आहे.
  (fluent but not a coherent poem)
```

`app/gradio_demo.py` serves this checkpoint as a chat UI (smoke-tested: server
starts, serves the chat API, returns real generations end-to-end). Honest
summary: the model reliably speaks fluent, grammatical Marathi and follows
the chat format after SFT, but factual accuracy and coherence at this
scale (42M params, 262M pretraining tokens, ~15k SFT examples) are limited -
exactly what the plan's "portfolio scale, not production quality" framing
predicts, not a bug to fix.

## Model tiers

| Tier | Params (measured) | Layers / Heads / d_model | Context |
|------|--------------------|---------------------------|---------|
| nano  | 22.9M (53.6% tied embedding) | 6 / 6 / 384  | 512  |
| small | 42.1M (38.9% tied embedding) | 8 / 8 / 512  | 1024 |
| base  | 109.5M (22.4% tied embedding) | 12 / 12 / 768 | 1024 |

Original targets were ~15M/~50M/~124M; actual counts run a bit higher for the
smaller tiers because the 32,000-word tokenizer's tied embedding table
(vocab_size × n_embd) is a fixed cost that dominates a narrow model
disproportionately - it shrinks from 54% of nano's params to 22% of base's
as d_model grows. Not a bug, just an artifact of picking the vocab size
before the model width.

# Veritas
Status: complete
One-liner: A GraphRAG engine combining vector and graph retrieval, containerized with GPU passthrough and running fully local.

Stack: ChromaDB, Neo4j, Ollama, Gemma, Docker Compose
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/Veritas

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
Vector retrieval is good at "find me something similar" and bad at "how are these two things connected" — multi-hop questions where the answer lives in a relationship rather than in any single chunk. Veritas pairs ChromaDB for semantic recall with a Neo4j entity graph for relational traversal, so both query shapes have a path to an answer. The deployment side was the part that took real work: Docker Compose with GPU passthrough to keep Ollama inference on the local card while Neo4j and Chroma run alongside it, reproducibly, on one machine.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)
- Stars: 0
- Last commit: 2026-07-28T20:23:21Z
- GitHub description: Privacy-first, self-hosted GraphRAG agent combining vector search (ChromaDB) with Neo4j knowledge-graph traversal for accurate, hallucination-resistant answers over technical documents — runs fully offline via Ollama and Docker.

## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub)
- Python: 45337
- JavaScript: 20257
- CSS: 12061
- HTML: 7850
- Dockerfile: 1007

## README
# Veritas

A privacy-first, self-hosted **GraphRAG** engine. Documents are chunked and embedded into a
vector store *and* mined for entities/relationships into a knowledge graph, so every answer
can point to the exact subgraph it traversed to get there — not just a wall of retrieved text.

- **Vector search** — ChromaDB, embeddings via local Ollama (`nomic-embed-text`)
- **Knowledge graph** — Neo4j, entities/relationships extracted per chunk by a local LLM
- **Answer generation** — Ollama (Gemma 3) by default; optionally Gemini or Groq if you provide an API key
- **Web UI** — Flask + Jinja2 + vanilla JS (vis-network, marked.js) — no build step

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U[Browser] -->|HTTP/SSE| FE[Flask webapp :8501]
    FE -->|proxy| API[FastAPI backend :8000]
    API --> CHROMA[(ChromaDB\nvector store)]
    API --> NEO4J[(Neo4j\nknowledge graph)]
    API --> OLLAMA[Ollama :11434\nGemma 3 / nomic-embed-text]
    API -.optional.-> GEMINI[Gemini API]
    API -.optional.-> GROQ[Groq API]
```

Question flow: the query is embedded and matched against Chroma; the chunks that come back are
used to seed a traversal into Neo4j (`Chunk -[:MENTIONS]-> Entity -[:RELATED_TO]-> Entity`); the
vector text + graph context are combined into a prompt and streamed back token-by-token, along
with the exact subgraph that was walked to build the answer.

## Ports

| Service | Container | Host port | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Web UI (Flask) | `frontend` | **8501** | main entrypoint |
| API (FastAPI) | `api` | **8000** | `/docs` for interactive Swagger UI |
| Neo4j Browser | `graph-db` | 7474 | `neo4j` / `veritas_password` |
| Neo4j Bolt | `graph-db` | 7687 | |
| Ollama | `llm-server` | 11434 | |
| ChromaDB (inspection only) | `vector-db` | 8001 | API talks to Chroma via a mounted local persist dir, not this port |

> The original Streamlit frontend called the API on port 8080 while the README documented 8000 —
> both the API and its Docker port mapping are now standardized on **8000**.

## Running it

### Docker Compose (recommended)

```bash
docker-compose up -d --build
```

Then open **http://localhost:8501**.

### Local dev (no Docker)

```bash
# terminal 1 - API (needs Neo4j + Ollama reachable at localhost)
cd backend
pip install -r requirements.txt
uvicorn main:app --reload --port 8000

# terminal 2 - web UI
cd webapp
pip install -r requirements.txt
export API_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000   # Windows: set API_BASE_URL=...
flask --app app.py run --port 8501
```

## Choosing an LLM provider

Answer generation defaults to the **local Ollama** model — nothing about your question or
retrieved context leaves the machine unless you opt in to a hosted API. Document ingestion
(entity/relationship extraction) always uses local Ollama regardless of this setting.

| Env var | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `LLM_PROVIDER` | `ollama` | `ollama` \| `gemini` \| `groq` |
| `OLLAMA_CHAT_MODEL` | `gemma3` | model served by the local Ollama container |
| `GEMINI_API_KEY` | — | required to use `gemini` |
| `GEMINI_MODEL` | `gemini-2.5-flash` | |
| `GROQ_API_KEY` | — | required to use `groq` |
| `GROQ_MODEL` | `llama-3.1-70b-versatile` | |

Per-request overrides are also supported — pass `"provider": "gemini"` (and optionally `"model"`)
in the JSON body of `/ask`, `/ask/stream`, or `/ask/compare` to use a different provider for a
single question without changing the default.

## API reference

| Method & path | Description |
|---|---|
| `GET /health` | Status of Neo4j, ChromaDB, Ollama, and the configured LLM providers |
| `POST /ask` | Non-streaming hybrid answer: `{query, provider?, model?, k?}` |
| `POST /ask/stream` | SSE token stream; final event carries sources, traversed subgraph, and timing |
| `POST /ask/compare` | Runs vector-only / graph-only / hybrid side by side |
| `GET /graph/overview?limit=200` | Sampled subgraph of the whole knowledge base, with counts |
| `GET /graph/node/{id}/neighbors` | Expand a node's neighbors (click-to-expand in the UI) |
| `POST /ingest/upload` | Upload a PDF/TXT/MD, runs the ingestion pipeline in the background |
| `GET /ingest/status/{job_id}` | Stage + running counts for an ingest job |
| `GET /documents` | List ingested documents with chunk/entity/relationship counts |
| `DELETE /documents/{name}` | Remove a document's chunks, vectors, and orphaned entities |

## Repo layout

```
backend/               FastAPI service
  main.py              API routes
  retrieval.py         shared vector + graph retrieval logic
  llm_providers.py     ollama / gemini / groq chat-model selection
  ingest.py            parsing -> chunking -> embedding -> entity extraction -> graph write
  test_api.py          endpoint smoke tests (mocked dependencies)
  test_agent.py        manual end-to-end script against a running API
webapp/                Flask UI (chat, ingest, graph explorer)
samples/               sample PDFs for trying out ingestion
docker-compose.yml
```

## Screenshots

_placeholder — add screenshots of the chat + graph panel, ingest progress, and explorer here._

---

Built by [Spandan Nagale](https://github.com/SpandanNagale).

# Self-Healing Hybrid RAG
Status: complete
One-liner: A hybrid retrieval pipeline that measures its own quality with RAGAS and repairs its index in the background when it degrades.

Stack: LangGraph, BM25, dense retrieval, RRF, cross-encoder reranking, RAGAS
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/self-healing-rag

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
Retrieval quality decays after deployment — documents change, the corpus grows, embeddings go stale — and most RAG systems have no idea it's happening because nothing measures them after the demo. The retrieval stack itself is conventional and deliberate: dense plus BM25 fused with reciprocal rank fusion to cover both semantic and lexical matching, then a cross-encoder rerank on the fused candidates to buy precision at the top. The part worth talking about is the layer above it — RAGAS evaluation running against the live system, and a background job that heals the index when scores drop, instead of waiting for a user to complain.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)
- Stars: 0
- Last commit: 2026-07-24T18:08:59Z
- GitHub description: A production-grade hybrid RAG system that detects its own retrieval failures and recovers automatically — combining vector search + page-level indexing with a self-correcting LangGraph pipeline that grades, retries, and verifies its own answers before responding

## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub)
- Python: 114026
- JavaScript: 16956
- CSS: 14419
- HTML: 6820

## README
# Self-Healing Hybrid RAG

A production-shaped Retrieval-Augmented Generation system built around two ideas:

1. **Hybrid retrieval** - every query fans out to a dense vector index (Qdrant) *and*
   a page/section-level keyword index (BM25) in parallel, fused with Reciprocal Rank
   Fusion and reranked with a cross-encoder.
2. **Self-healing** - a [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) state
   machine grades its own retrieval quality and verifies its own answers against the
   retrieved context. When either check fails, it rewrites the query, widens context,
   or switches retrieval strategy - and only gives up with an explicit
   "insufficient context" if every recovery strategy is exhausted. It never silently
   hallucinates past a bad retrieval.

A separate background job mines the failure history this loop produces to find
documents that are *repeatedly* graded low-relevance, and automatically
re-chunks them with a different strategy - fixing bad ingestion decisions
without a human in the loop.

---

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Ingestion["Ingestion Pipeline"]
        direction TB
        U[Upload: PDF / DOCX / TXT / MD] --> P[Parse: pages, sections, tables]
        P --> H[Content hash per page/chunk]
        H --> C[Chunk: sliding window, configurable size/overlap]
        C --> V1[(Qdrant\nvector path)]
        P --> K1[(BM25\npage/section index)]
        H -. "unchanged hash -> skip re-embed" .-> V1
        H -. "unchanged hash -> skip re-tokenize" .-> K1
    end

    subgraph Query["Self-Healing Query Loop  (LangGraph)"]
        direction TB
        R[Retrieve\nhybrid: vector + keyword] --> RRF[RRF fusion + cross-encoder rerank]
        RRF --> G{Grade relevance}
        G -- relevant --> GEN[Generate\ngrounded answer + citations]
        G -- "low relevance\n(retries left)" --> RW[Rewrite / expand query]
        RW --> R
        G -- "retries exhausted" --> WS[Widen context /\nswitch vector<->keyword]
        WS --> G
        G -- "all strategies exhausted" --> INSUF[Return: insufficient context]
        GEN --> VER{Verify faithfulness}
        VER -- supported --> DONE[Return answer]
        VER -- "unsupported\n(retries left)" --> GEN2[Regenerate,\nstricter grounding]
        GEN2 --> VER
        VER -- "verify retries exhausted" --> RW
        INSUF --> DONE
    end

    Query -. "every low-relevance grade / failed verify" .-> FL[(Failure log\nJSONL)]

    subgraph Healing["Index Healing  (background job)"]
        direction TB
        FL --> AN[Analyze: count failures per doc_id]
        AN -- "doc exceeds\nfailure threshold" --> RC[Re-chunk + re-embed\nthat doc only, smaller chunk size]
        RC --> V1
        RC --> K1
    end

    V1 --> R
    K1 --> R
```

### Why this design

- **Two indexes, not one.** Dense vectors are great at paraphrase/semantic
  matches but blur exact numbers, table cells, and rare terms. A page-level
  BM25 index keeps those intact. RRF fusion means neither path has to be
  perfect alone.
- **The graph grades and verifies itself.** Most RAG demos assume retrieval
  worked and generation is grounded. This one checks both, explicitly, with
  the LLM acting as its own critic - and has a real recovery path (rewrite →
  widen/switch → give up honestly) instead of one shot at an answer.
- **Failure logs feed back into ingestion.** A single bad answer might just be
  a hard question. A document that shows up in low-relevance grades across
  many *different* queries is a chunking problem, not a question problem -
  that's the signal the index-healing job looks for.
- **Everything provider-specific is config, not code.** LLM and embedding
  providers are swapped via `.env` - see [Configuration](#configuration).

---

## Repo layout

```
app/
  config.py                 # pydantic-settings, env-driven
  dependencies.py           # wires every singleton together (Container)
  main.py                   # FastAPI app + lifespan (starts index-healing loop)
  models/schemas.py          # shared pydantic models (Chunk, RetrievedChunk, QueryResponse, ...)
  ingestion/
    parsers.py               # PDF (pdfplumber) / DOCX (python-docx) / text+markdown
    chunking.py              # sliding-window word chunker
    hashing.py                # content hashes -> incremental indexing
    registry.py                # per-doc metadata (storage path, chunk size used)
    pipeline.py                 # ties parse -> chunk -> diff -> index together
  embeddings/                 # local (sentence-transformers) | ollama | gemini
  llm/                         # ollama | ollama_cloud | gemini | groq
  retrieval/
    vector_store.py           # Qdrant wrapper (embedded-mode by default)
    keyword_store.py           # BM25 page-level index
    fusion.py                    # Reciprocal Rank Fusion
    reranker.py                   # cross-encoder reranking
    hybrid.py                      # ties it all together + widen/switch fallbacks
  graph/
    state.py, nodes.py, graph.py, prompts.py, runner.py   # the LangGraph state machine
  healing/
    failure_logger.py          # structured JSONL of every retry/failure
    index_healer.py              # analyzes failures, re-chunks bad docs
    scheduler.py                  # runs index_healer on an interval
  cache/semantic_cache.py     # embedding-similarity query cache
  observability/               # structured logging + RAGAS-style proxy metrics
  api/                           # FastAPI routers: /ingest, /query, /health, /metrics
tests/                           # pytest suite, incl. the self-healing demo scenario
scripts/run_demo.py             # narrated end-to-end demo against your real LLM
```

---

## Setup

### 1. Install dependencies

```bash
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate        # Windows
# source .venv/bin/activate   # macOS/Linux

pip install -r requirements.txt
```

### 2. Configure providers

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

By default the system runs **entirely locally, no API keys required**:
- LLM: `ollama` (`qwen2.5:14b`) - install [Ollama](https://ollama.com), then:
  ```bash
  ollama pull qwen2.5:14b
  ollama serve
  ```
- Embeddings: `local` sentence-transformers (`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`), downloaded
  automatically on first run.
- Vector store: embedded/on-disk Qdrant (`./data/qdrant`) - no server needed.
- Keyword index: pure-Python BM25 (`rank_bm25`) - no server needed.

To use a hosted provider instead, edit `.env`:

| Setting | Options |
|---|---|
| `LLM_PROVIDER` | `ollama` (local) · `ollama_cloud` (hosted, needs `OLLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY`) · `gemini` (needs `GEMINI_API_KEY`) · `groq` (needs `GROQ_API_KEY`) |
| `EMBEDDING_PROVIDER` | `local` (sentence-transformers) · `ollama` (local or cloud) · `gemini` |
| `QDRANT_URL` | leave empty for embedded mode, or point at a running Qdrant server |

Chunk sizes, retry limits, top-k, and cache thresholds are all in `.env` too -
see `.env.example` for the full list with comments.

### 3. Run the API + web UI

```bash
uvicorn app.main:app --reload
```

Then open **http://localhost:8000/** for the web UI (screenshots below), or
use the API directly:

- `POST /ingest` - multipart file upload (`file=@doc.pdf`), returns immediately
  with `{"doc_id", "status": "queued"}` while parsing/embedding happens in a
  background task.
- `GET /ingest/status/{doc_id}` - check whether a queued document has finished indexing.
- `GET /documents` / `DELETE /documents/{doc_id}` - list / remove ingested documents.
- `POST /query` - `{"query": "...", "doc_id": "optional-scope-to-one-doc"}`,
  returns the final `QueryResponse` in one shot.
- `POST /query/stream` - same pipeline, but pushed to the client node-by-node
  over Server-Sent Events as the graph actually executes (`data: {"type":
  "step", "node": "grade", "grade": "irrelevant", ...}` for each step, then a
  final `{"type": "final", ...}` with the full `QueryResponse`). This is what
  the web UI's live trace panel consumes - it is not a replay or animation,
  each event is emitted the moment that graph node finishes.
- `GET /config` / `POST /config` - read/update the active LLM and embedding
  provider+model at runtime (see [Web UI](#web-ui) below for the caveats around
  changing embeddings).
- `GET /config/ollama-models?cloud=false` - lists models actually available on
  the configured Ollama host, for the UI's model picker.
- `GET /health` - current provider config.
- `GET /metrics` - query counts, cache hit rate, faithfulness/relevance proxy
  metrics, retrieval-strategy usage.

## Web UI

A single-page UI (`static/index.html` + `style.css` + `app.js`, no build
step, no framework - served directly by FastAPI's `StaticFiles`) is designed
so someone with no RAG background can watch the self-healing loop happen and
understand *why* each step occurred, not just see a final answer:

- **Documents panel** - drag-and-drop upload, live indexed/queued status,
  per-document page/chunk counts, remove button.
- **Ask panel** - a question box and an optional "scope to one document" picker.
- **"How it's thinking" panel** - the real live trace from `/query/stream`,
  translated into plain language per step ("Rewriting the question (attempt
  1)... retrieval wasn't good enough, so the query is being reformulated to:
  ...", "Double-checking the answer... ✅ Fully supported by the retrieved
  passages."), color-coded by outcome (relevant/verified = green, retry in
  progress = amber, gave up = red).
- **Answer panel** - the grounded answer, citation chips (doc + page +
  section), and the retry count / strategy used / verification result for
  that specific answer.
- **System health panel** - live `/metrics` snapshot (query count, cache hit
  rate, faithfulness proxy, average retries).
- **Provider settings drawer** - switch LLM provider (Ollama local / Ollama
  Cloud / Gemini / Groq) and model at runtime, with an Ollama model picker
  populated from whatever's actually pulled on the configured host. Embedding
  provider/model can also be changed here, but since a different embedding
  model means an incompatible vector space, doing so **clears the vector
  index, keyword index, and document registry** and requires re-ingesting -
  the UI shows this warning before/after applying the change.

Visual style is a "liquid glass" look: translucent, blurred glass panels
(`backdrop-filter: blur() saturate()`) over an animated dark gradient
background, consistent across every panel and the settings drawer.

| Initial state | Answer + live trace | Provider settings |
|---|---|---|
| ![Initial state](docs/screenshots/01_initial.png) | ![Answer and trace](docs/screenshots/02_answer.png) | ![Provider settings drawer](docs/screenshots/03_settings.png) |

### 4. Run the tests

```bash
pytest
```

The test suite uses fake (offline, deterministic) embedding and LLM providers
so it runs without Ollama, API keys, or model downloads - see `tests/fakes.py`.

---

## The self-healing loop, demonstrated

### Guaranteed-deterministic version (CI)

```bash
pytest tests/test_self_healing_demo.py -v
```

`test_self_healing_recovers_after_failed_first_retrieval` ingests a short
policy document and asks a question phrased with vocabulary that shares no
terms with the source text ("money back timeframe" vs. a document that talks
about "refunds... processed... business days"). Walking through what actually
happens:

1. **Retrieve** (hybrid, original query) - BM25 finds zero token overlap; the
   embedding path returns only weak matches.
2. **Grade** - flagged `irrelevant`. Logged to the failure log.
3. **Rewrite** - query becomes `"refund business days processing time"`.
4. **Retrieve** (hybrid, rewritten query) - now BM25 and vector search both
   land on the *Refund Policy* section.
5. **Grade** - `relevant`.
6. **Generate** - grounded answer with an inline citation.
7. **Verify** - answer checked against the retrieved passage, passes.

Final response: `retries=1`, `insufficient_context=False`, answer contains
the correct figure, citation points at the right page. A second test in the
same file (`test_query_that_never_recovers_returns_insufficient_context`)
proves the other half of the contract: when nothing in the corpus is
relevant, the system returns an explicit "insufficient context" message
instead of guessing.

### Real end-to-end version (your configured LLM)

```bash
python scripts/run_demo.py
```

Runs the same shape of scenario against whatever LLM/embedding provider is in
your `.env` (local Ollama by default), against a small travel-expense policy
doc with a deliberate decoy section, and prints the full node-by-node trace.
Because it's a real model instead of a scripted one, the exact retry count can
vary run to run - that's expected and is why the pytest version above is the
reproducible source of truth.

### Index healing

`tests/test_index_healing.py` shows the other half of the self-healing story:
after a document accumulates enough low-relevance grades across different
queries (`INDEX_HEALING_FAILURE_THRESHOLD`, default 3), the background job
(`app/healing/index_healer.py`) re-chunks and re-embeds *that document only*
with a smaller chunk size - without touching any other document in the index,
and without a query ever asking for it directly.

---

## Configuration reference

See `.env.example` for the complete, commented list. Key knobs:

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `CHUNK_SIZE` / `CHUNK_OVERLAP` | Word-count sliding window for the vector path |
| `RETRIEVAL_TOP_K` / `RERANK_TOP_K` | Candidates fused per path / kept after reranking |
| `MAX_REWRITE_RETRIES` | How many times the graph rewrites+re-retrieves before falling back to widen/switch |
| `MAX_VERIFY_RETRIES` | How many times generation is retried with stricter grounding before falling back to a retrieval retry |
| `GRADE_RELEVANCE_THRESHOLD` | Reserved for a future numeric grader; current grader is categorical (relevant/partial/irrelevant) |
| `INDEX_HEALING_INTERVAL_SECONDS` | How often the background healing job runs |
| `INDEX_HEALING_FAILURE_THRESHOLD` | Low-relevance grades (across distinct queries) before a doc gets re-chunked |
| `SEMANTIC_CACHE_THRESHOLD` | Cosine similarity above which a query is treated as a cache hit |

## Known limitations

- BM25 index rebuilds its ranking structure on every write (cheap - it skips
  re-tokenizing unchanged pages, but there's no true incremental posting-list
  update like a real search engine would have).
- Embedded Qdrant (file-backed, no server) is single-process; point
  `QDRANT_URL` at a real Qdrant deployment for multi-worker/production use.
- Metrics are proxies computed from the graph's own grade/verify calls, not
  full RAGAS (which would require its own separate LLM-judge calls per query).
- Ingestion runs as an in-process `BackgroundTasks` job, not a durable queue -
  a process restart mid-ingestion loses that job (acceptable for this scope;
  swap in Celery+Redis if you need durability across restarts).
